top5.rationale: Dog bite in an asplenic-appearing patient (small spleen with granulomas) with alcohol abuse, rapid purpura fulminans, DIC, and multiorgan failure is classic.

top5.diagnosis: Pasteurella multocida sepsis
top5.rationale: Dog bite exposure with rapid soft-tissue infection, livedo, and shock; less fulminant than Capnocytophaga but fits the zoonotic bite narrative.

top5.diagnosis: Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (Streptococcus pyogenes)
top5.rationale: Necrotic-edged wounds, rapidly progressive purpura, shock, and multiorgan failure could reflect invasive group A streptococcal infection from skin breaches.

top5.diagnosis: Alcohol withdrawal with delirium tremens and aspiration pneumonia
top5.rationale: 18 beers daily, stopped 3 days prior, now confused/agitated with respiratory failure and pulmonary opacities; a hidden driver of the acute decompensation.

top5.diagnosis: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease)
top5.rationale: Occupational exposure installing air-conditioning systems and dog contact could expose to contaminated water/urine; jaundice, renal failure, and pulmonary hemorrhage fit, though not classic for purpura fulminans.

top5.diagnosis: Statin-induced necrotizing autoimmune myopathy (HMGCR antibody-associated)
top5.rationale: Subacute proximal weakness with fatigue, dyspnea, and dramatic CK elevation (5358) on atorvastatin, with facial/periorbital edema and hoarseness from pharyngeal weakness; the statin was stopped and CK should be trended.

top5.diagnosis: Hypothyroid myopathy with myxedema (including possible myxedema effusion/edema)
top5.rationale: History of hypothyroidism, facial puffiness, periorbital edema, hoarseness, fatigue, and weight gain with elevated CK all fit; TSH was normal 8 months ago but may now be elevated.

top5.diagnosis: Dermatomyositis or polymyositis (inflammatory myopathy)
top5.rationale: Proximal weakness, dyspnea, hoarseness, and marked CK elevation fit an inflammatory myopathy; family history of sarcoidosis and prior benign lung nodule add autoimmune context.

top5.diagnosis: Superior vena cava syndrome from occult malignancy (e.g., lung cancer or mediastinal mass)
top5.rationale: Facial puffiness, periorbital edema, hoarseness, and dyspnea could reflect venous obstruction or recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement; chest radiograph showed no mass, but CT may be needed.

top5.diagnosis: Sarcoidosis with myopathy and/or mediastinal involvement
top5.rationale: Family history of sarcoidosis, reticulonodular right basilar opacities, and systemic symptoms including fatigue, dyspnea, and facial swelling could represent sarcoid myopathy or nodal disease.

top5.diagnosis: Statin-induced necrotizing autoimmune myopathy (anti-HMGCR antibody positive)
top5.rationale: Atorvastatin exposure with markedly elevated CK (5358), AST/ALT elevation, progressive fatigue and dyspnea without myalgias; NAM is the classic statin-triggered myopathy and can cause pharyngeal weakness (hoarseness) and facial edema from associated myocarditis or capillary leak.

top5.diagnosis: Hypothyroid myopathy (statin-exacerbated) with myxedema
top5.rationale: Known hypothyroidism on levothyroxine with facial/periorbital puffiness, hoarseness, weight gain, and CK elevation; myxedema can produce the constellation of edema, hoarseness, and fatigue, and statins unmask or worsen myopathy in hypothyroid states.

top5.diagnosis: Superior vena cava syndrome from occult malignancy (e.g., lung cancer or mediastinal mass)
top5.rationale: Facial puffiness, periorbital edema, hoarseness, and dyspnea suggest venous obstruction; the prior right middle lobe lobectomy for a spiculated nodule and reticulonodular right basilar opacities raise concern for recurrent or new thoracic malignancy despite negative chest radiograph.

top5.diagnosis: Dermatomyositis or polymyositis (paraneoplastic or idiopathic)
top5.rationale: Proximal weakness, dyspnea, hoarseness, and marked CK elevation fit inflammatory myopathy; family history of sarcoidosis and prior smoking raise concern for underlying malignancy or granulomatous myopathy, and facial edema can occur with dermatomyositis.

top5.diagnosis: Amyloidosis (AL or AA) with myopathy and soft-tissue infiltration
top5.rationale: Facial/periorbital swelling, hoarseness, fatigue, and renal dysfunction could reflect amyloid infiltration of muscle, skin, and kidney; CK elevation is atypical but can occur with amyloid myopathy, and this is easily overlooked in a patient with chronic kidney disease and monoclonal gammopathy risk.

top5.diagnosis: Statin-induced necrotizing autoimmune myopathy (anti-HMGCR)
top5.rationale: CK 5358 with AST>ALT, normal CRP, and recent atorvastatin exposure fits this statin-triggered myopathy; facial/periorbital edema and hoarseness could reflect pharyngeal/cervical muscle weakness, and it is easily overlooked because statins were stopped and symptoms attributed to other causes.

top5.diagnosis: Hypothyroid myopathy with myxedema (levothyroxine nonadherence or under-replacement)
top5.rationale: Hoarseness, facial puffiness, periorbital edema, weight gain, fatigue, and marked CK elevation are classic for hypothyroid myopathy; the normal TSH 8 months earlier does not exclude interval development, and this unifies the edema, voice change, and enzyme pattern.

top5.diagnosis: Dermatomyositis or polymyositis (inflammatory myopathy)
top5.rationale: Proximal weakness with fatigue, dyspnea, hoarseness, and CK >5000 with AST/ALT elevation fit an inflammatory myopathy; normal CRP is atypical but does not exclude it, and the family history of sarcoidosis raises autoimmune susceptibility.

top5.diagnosis: Superior vena cava syndrome from occult malignancy or aortic pathology
top5.rationale: Facial and periorbital swelling, hoarseness, and dyspnea raise concern for SVC obstruction; the chest radiograph showed no mediastinal mass, but the known abdominal aortic aneurysm and prior smoldering findings warrant cross-sectional imaging, and this is a can't-miss diagnosis.

top5.diagnosis: Recurrent aspiration pneumonitis with reactive airway disease
top5.rationale: Reticulonodular right basilar opacities, esophageal motility disorder, GERD, and hoarseness suggest chronic aspiration; this could explain the cough, dyspnea, and radiographic pattern, though it does not account for the CK elevation or facial edema.

top5.diagnosis: Statin-induced necrotizing autoimmune myopathy (anti-HMGCR antibody positive)
top5.rationale: Recent atorvastatin exposure with markedly elevated CK (5358), normal inflammatory markers, and progressive proximal weakness/fatigue fits this increasingly recognized entity in elderly patients.

top5.diagnosis: Hypothyroidism-related myopathy and myxedema (with possible statin interaction)
top5.rationale: History of hypothyroidism on levothyroxine with facial/periorbital edema, hoarseness, weight gain, fatigue, and elevated CK; hypothyroidism can both cause myopathy and predispose to statin myotoxicity.

top5.diagnosis: Superior vena cava syndrome from occult malignancy (e.g., lung cancer or mediastinal mass)
top5.rationale: Facial puffiness, periorbital edema, hoarseness, and abdominal swelling in an elderly former smoker with prior lung nodule raise concern for SVC obstruction, though chest imaging showed no mass.

top5.diagnosis: Dermatomyositis or polymyositis (paraneoplastic or idiopathic)
top5.rationale: Proximal muscle weakness, elevated CK, and family history of sarcoidosis (autoimmune diathesis) support inflammatory myopathy; normal ESR/CRP does not exclude it.

top5.diagnosis: Recurrent aspiration pneumonitis with reactive airway disease
top5.rationale: Esophageal motility disorder, GERD, prior pneumonia, and right middle lobe lobectomy with reticulonodular right basilar opacities suggest chronic aspiration contributing to hoarseness and cough.

top5.diagnosis: Severe community-acquired pneumonia due to Staphylococcus aureus (including Panton-Valentine leukocidin–positive MRSA) with toxic shock syndrome and acute respiratory distress syndrome
top5.rationale: Rapidly progressive necrotizing pneumonia with cavitary/nodular consolidations, bloody secretions, leukopenia with bandemia and atypical lymphocytes, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, shock, and multiorgan failure in a previously healthy young adult best fits PVL-positive S. aureus pneumonia with toxin-mediated shock.

top5.diagnosis: Influenza pneumonia with secondary bacterial coinfection (e.g., S. aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae) and septic shock
top5.rationale: Winter presentation with a viral prodrome followed by abrupt deterioration, diffuse nodular consolidations, leukopenia, and shock is classic for influenza with secondary bacterial pneumonia, though the degree of leukopenia and rapid ARDS favors a toxin-mediated superinfection.

top5.diagnosis: Fulminant viral myocarditis (e.g., influenza or enterovirus) with cardiogenic shock and ARDS
top5.rationale: Bedside echocardiography showed diffuse decreased cardiac function and reduced ejection fraction without right ventricular enlargement, supporting a primary myocardial process contributing to shock, though the nodular pulmonary consolidations and bloody secretions are more typical of pneumonia.

top5.diagnosis: Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy with acute respiratory distress syndrome due to severe community-acquired bacterial pneumonia
top5.rationale: The combination of refractory shock, diffuse bilateral consolidations, and reduced ejection fraction on echocardiography is consistent with sepsis-related myocardial depression, but this is likely a complication rather than the unifying primary diagnosis.

top5.diagnosis: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome
top5.rationale: A previously healthy young man with a febrile prodrome progressing to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, shock, and leukocytosis with atypical lymphocytes could fit hantavirus, but the absence of a rodent exposure, the nodular consolidations, and the winter/urban setting make this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Statin-induced necrotizing autoimmune myopathy (anti-HMGCR) with associated dysphagia and possible aspiration
top5.rationale: Markedly elevated CK (5358) with subacute proximal weakness/fatigue, recent atorvastatin exposure, and hoarseness/dyspnea could reflect pharyngeal weakness rather than a primary airway or thyroid process; the facial edema may be from hypoalbuminemia or venous congestion, and this unifying myopathic explanation is easily overlooked when the presentation is framed around sore throat and hoarseness.

top5.diagnosis: Hypothyroidism (severe/untreated) with myxedema causing hoarseness, facial/periorbital edema, fatigue, and elevated CK
top5.rationale: The patient has known hypothyroidism on levothyroxine, and hypothyroidism can produce hoarseness, facial puffiness, weight gain, fatigue, and marked CK elevation; a normal TSH 8 months earlier does not exclude interval development of overt hypothyroidism, and this single endocrine explanation accounts for many findings without invoking a new systemic disease.

top5.diagnosis: Superior vena cava syndrome from an occult mediastinal process (e.g., lung cancer, lymphoma, or aortic aneurysm-related compression)
top5.rationale: Facial and periorbital swelling, hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement), and dyspnea raise concern for impaired venous return or mediastinal mass; chest radiographs reportedly showed no mediastinal mass, but this does not fully exclude a small or non-radiographically obvious lesion, and the absence of dyspnea early on makes this less likely but still dangerous to miss.

top5.diagnosis: Recurrent aspiration pneumonitis with reactive airway/upper airway symptoms due to esophageal motility disorder and GERD
top5.rationale: Known esophageal motility disorder and GERD, prior aspiration-related right basilar scarring, and new cough with white mucus and hoarseness fit recurrent aspiration; this could explain the reticulonodular right basilar opacities and respiratory symptoms without requiring a new systemic inflammatory or neoplastic process.

top5.diagnosis: Depression-related somatic symptom amplification and deconditioning with medication effects (e.g., citalopram, levothyroxine, or statin intolerance)
top5.rationale: The patient has a history of depression and lives alone; fatigue, hoarseness, and edema may be amplified or perpetuated by mood disorder and deconditioning, while medications such as citalopram and atorvastatin can contribute to fatigue and muscle symptoms, making a primarily psychiatric/medication-related explanation a plausible alternative that could be overlooked.

top5.diagnosis: Influenza pneumonia with concomitant Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia and toxic shock syndrome
top5.rationale: Winter influenza prodrome followed by rapid necrotizing pneumonia, cavitary/nodular consolidations, bloody secretions, leukopenia with bandemia and atypical lymphocytes, thrombocytopenia, DIC, shock, and multiorgan failure fits post-influenza S. aureus coinfection with toxin-mediated shock.

top5.diagnosis: Fulminant community-acquired necrotizing pneumonia due to Panton-Valentine leukocidin-positive Staphylococcus aureus
top5.rationale: PVL-positive S. aureus can cause fulminant hemorrhagic necrotizing pneumonia with nodular consolidations, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, DIC, and shock even without antecedent influenza, and is easily overlooked when blood cultures are initially sterile.

top5.diagnosis: Influenza pneumonia with secondary invasive pneumococcal disease and purpura fulminans
top5.rationale: Influenza predisposes to Streptococcus pneumoniae coinfection, which can produce lobar/nodular consolidation, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, and shock; pneumococcal purpura fulminans would explain the mottled ashen skin and DIC.

top5.diagnosis: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome
top5.rationale: A viral prodrome followed by rapid noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, shock, leukocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, thrombocytopenia, hemoconcentration, and renal dysfunction could mimic this presentation, though the nodular consolidations and bloody secretions are less typical.

top5.diagnosis: Leptospirosis with severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome and septic shock
top5.rationale: Occupational spray-painting exposure could involve contaminated water; leptospirosis can cause fever, myalgias, diarrhea, renal failure, thrombocytopenia, DIC, and severe pulmonary hemorrhage with nodular infiltrates, and is a classic overlooked zoonosis.

top5.diagnosis: Influenza pneumonia with secondary Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia and toxic shock syndrome
top5.rationale: Winter onset, rapid progression from clear CXR to nodular/cavitary consolidations, leukopenia with bandemia and atypical lymphocytes, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, shock, and bloody secretions fit fulminant influenza with S. aureus coinfection and toxin-mediated shock.

top5.diagnosis: Influenza A (H1N1) viral pneumonia with acute respiratory distress syndrome and septic shock
top5.rationale: Primary viral pneumonitis can cause bilateral nodular consolidations, severe hypoxemia, leukopenia, and multiorgan failure; the winter cluster and rapid deterioration support this, though bacterial superinfection is more typical.

top5.diagnosis: Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteremic pneumonia with purpura fulminans and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
top5.rationale: Overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis can present with shock, DIC, thrombocytopenia, and bilateral consolidations, but the nodular pattern and leukopenia are less typical.

top5.diagnosis: Legionella pneumophila pneumonia with shock and rhabdomyolysis
top5.rationale: Legionnaires' disease can cause severe pneumonia, diarrhea, hyponatremia, elevated AST, and shock, but the marked leukopenia and nodular cavitary pattern are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia with acute respiratory distress syndrome in undiagnosed HIV infection
top5.rationale: Diffuse bilateral infiltrates, severe hypoxemia, and leukopenia could fit, but the negative HIV test, acute winter onset, and nodular consolidations make this unlikely.

top5.diagnosis: Influenza pneumonia with secondary Staphylococcus aureus co-infection (including possible necrotizing pneumonia and toxic shock syndrome)
top5.rationale: Winter onset, rapid progression from bronchitis to shock with nodular consolidations, leukopenia with bandemia and atypical lymphocytes, thrombocytopenia, and bloody secretions fit fulminant influenza with S. aureus superinfection better than most alternatives.

top5.diagnosis: Inhalational anthrax (Bacillus anthracis)
top5.rationale: Recent spray-painting exposure, rapid progression to shock with diffuse nodular consolidations, and hemorrhagic respiratory secretions are classic for inhalational anthrax, which a non-infectious-disease specialist might overlook.

top5.diagnosis: Leptospirosis (severe pulmonary hemorrhagic form, Weil disease)
top5.rationale: Explains fever, shock, renal failure, thrombocytopenia, hemoptysis, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates; exposure history is less clear but water/soil contact during spray painting could be relevant.

top5.diagnosis: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome
top5.rationale: Fits rapidly progressive pulmonary edema/consolidation, shock, leukocytosis with atypical lymphocytes, thrombocytopenia, and elevated LDH, though winter and lack of rodent exposure are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Toxic shock syndrome from a non-staphylococcal source (e.g., streptococcal toxic shock syndrome)
top5.rationale: Explains shock, fever, rash-like mottling, renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and rapid respiratory decline, but lacks a clear portal of entry and does not fully account for the nodular pulmonary pattern.

top5.diagnosis: Meconium aspiration syndrome with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE)
top5.rationale: The initial presentation of meconium-stained fluid, respiratory distress, and PPHN is classic; however, the extreme macrosomia, hypernatremia, and progressive neurologic findings suggest a more complex underlying disorder.

top5.diagnosis: Neonatal sepsis with meningitis (e.g., group B Streptococcus or Escherichia coli)
top5.rationale: Maternal fever, meconium staining, hypotension, and lethargy are consistent with sepsis; however, the negative maternal GBS screen and lack of positive cultures make this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Inborn error of metabolism (e.g., urea cycle disorder or organic acidemia)
top5.rationale: Hypernatremia, hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, and neurologic deterioration could be explained by a metabolic disorder, but the absence of a family history and the acute perinatal course make this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Neonatal stroke or intracranial hemorrhage
top5.rationale: The sudden neurologic deterioration, seizures, and full fontanelle could indicate a vascular event, but the initial respiratory distress and PPHN are not typical.

top5.diagnosis: Congenital myotonic dystrophy
top5.rationale: Macrosomia, hypotonia, and respiratory distress could suggest this, but the hypernatremia and hypertonia later are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Influenza pneumonia with Staphylococcus aureus coinfection (including necrotizing/pneumonia with toxic shock syndrome)
top5.rationale: Winter onset, rapid progression to shock and ARDS, bloody respiratory secretions, leukopenia with band forms, and nodular consolidations fit post-influenza S. aureus superinfection; recent spray-painting exposure does not exclude this.

top5.diagnosis: Severe community-acquired pneumonia due to Streptococcus pneumoniae with septic shock and purpura fulminans
top5.rationale: Abrupt deterioration, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, and multilobar consolidation are compatible with invasive pneumococcal disease, though the nodular pattern and bloody secretions are less typical.

top5.diagnosis: Hydrocarbon pneumonitis with secondary bacterial pneumonia and ARDS
top5.rationale: Recent spray painting buildings is a hidden occupational exposure to volatile hydrocarbons; aspiration or inhalation can cause acute pneumonitis, nodular opacities, and rapid respiratory failure, with bacterial superinfection driving shock.

top5.diagnosis: Leptospirosis (Weil disease) with pulmonary hemorrhage and shock
top5.rationale: Exposure to contaminated water or animal reservoirs during spray-painting work could explain fever, myalgias, diarrhea, jaundice, renal failure, thrombocytopenia, and pulmonary hemorrhage, though anicteric presentation is possible.

top5.diagnosis: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome
top5.rationale: Aerosolized rodent excreta exposure during building spray-painting could cause a winter prodrome, rapid noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, shock, leukocytosis, and thrombocytopenia, but the nodular consolidations and bloody secretions are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Primary CNS lymphoma
top5.rationale: Partially enhancing, irregularly marginated mass with leptomeningeal nodules along pons/medulla in an immunocompetent young adult is classic for PCNSL, and normal spectroscopy/perfusion does not exclude it.

top5.diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis
top5.rationale: Leptomeningeal enhancement, cranial nerve/parenchymal involvement, and African-American ancestry fit sarcoidosis, though systemic features are absent.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis with tuberculoma
top5.rationale: Leptomeningeal nodules and basal meningeal enhancement can mimic TB, but no fever, travel, or CSF data are provided.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic malignancy (e.g., melanoma, lung, breast)
top5.rationale: Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis with parenchymal mass can present this way, but no primary tumor or systemic symptoms are evident.

top5.diagnosis: Autoimmune/paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis
top5.rationale: Olfactory hallucinations and temporal lobe FLAIR changes suggest limbic involvement, but the discrete enhancing mass and leptomeningeal nodules are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis
top5.rationale: Leptomeningeal nodular enhancement along basilar cisterns, medulla, and temporal lobe with normal spectroscopy/perfusion fits granulomatous meningitis, and the negative systemic review does not exclude isolated CNS sarcoid.

top5.diagnosis: Primary CNS lymphoma
top5.rationale: Partially enhancing, irregular periventricular/leptomeningeal mass with insular and basal ganglia FLAIR extension is classic, though normal MR spectroscopy and perfusion are atypical and may reflect steroid effect or low tumor burden.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
top5.rationale: Nodular leptomeningeal enhancement along the basis pontis and medulla is a hallmark of TB meningitis; the patient's African-American/Caribbean ancestry raises pretest probability despite no reported travel.

top5.diagnosis: Neurocysticercosis
top5.rationale: Multiple enhancing leptomeningeal nodules in a patient of Caribbean ancestry could represent racemose or subarachnoid cysticercosis, an infectious cause easily overlooked without dedicated CSF serology or travel history.

top5.diagnosis: Focal cortical dysplasia with secondary leptomeningeal enhancement (incidental)
top5.rationale: The long-standing olfactory hallucinations and left-sided paresthesias suggest a structural epileptogenic lesion; the enhancing leptomeningeal nodules may be an incidental companion finding rather than the primary diagnosis.

top5.diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis
top5.rationale: Young African-American man with leptomeningeal nodular enhancement along temporal lobe, pons, and medulla; olfactory hallucinations and paresthesias fit granulomatous meningeal involvement, and cardiac voltage criteria for LVH may signal subclinical cardiac sarcoid.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis with tuberculoma
top5.rationale: Leptomeningeal nodules and basilar meningeal enhancement are classic for TB, and Caribbean ancestry raises exposure risk despite no reported travel; indolent course over one year fits.

top5.diagnosis: Primary CNS lymphoma
top5.rationale: Partially enhancing periventricular/leptomeningeal mass in an immunocompetent young adult; normal spectroscopy does not exclude lymphoma, and leptomeningeal spread along pons and medulla is characteristic.

top5.diagnosis: Neurocysticercosis
top5.rationale: Olfactory hallucinations, focal seizures, and nodular enhancing lesions with leptomeningeal involvement could reflect parasitic cysts; Caribbean ancestry is a risk factor even without recent travel.

top5.diagnosis: IgG4-related hypertrophic pachymeningitis
top5.rationale: Multifocal nodular leptomeningeal enhancement involving temporal lobe, pons, and medulla can be an immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disorder; another specialist might overlook this because systemic features are absent.

top5.diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis
top5.rationale: Noncaseating granulomatous inflammation can produce nodular leptomeningeal and parenchymal enhancement along the temporal lobe, pons, and medulla, with olfactory hallucinations from temporal/insular involvement and paresthesias from brainstem or cortical spread; normal spectroscopy/perfusion and systemic quiescence fit.

top5.diagnosis: Primary CNS lymphoma
top5.rationale: Perivascular and leptomeningeal infiltration by malignant lymphocytes can mimic nodular enhancing masses with minimal FLAIR change and normal spectroscopy; immunocompetent young adults can present this way, though systemic symptoms are absent.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis with tuberculoma
top5.rationale: Mycobacterial leptomeningeal disease can cause nodular enhancement along basal cisterns, pons, and medulla with adjacent parenchymal signal change; olfactory and brainstem symptoms fit, and Caribbean ancestry raises exposure risk despite no travel history.

top5.diagnosis: Neurocysticercosis
top5.rationale: Parenchymal and subarachnoid cysts with nodular enhancement can occur along the temporal lobe and brainstem; seizures and focal deficits fit, though the absence of typical cystic lesions and no travel to endemic areas lowers likelihood.

top5.diagnosis: Rosai-Dorfman disease (isolated CNS)
top5.rationale: Histiocytic proliferation can form dural/leptomeningeal-based enhancing masses mimicking meningioma or granulomatous disease; isolated CNS involvement is rare but can explain nodular enhancement without systemic findings.

top5.diagnosis: Epstein–Barr virus encephalitis with cerebellitis and right otomastoiditis
top5.rationale: Unifying post-EBV infectious mononucleosis with cerebellar/vestibular and cognitive dysfunction, CSF lymphocytosis, and contiguous right ear/mastoid disease; the most parsimonious single explanation.

top5.diagnosis: Post-infectious cerebellitis (EBV-associated) with incidental right otomastoiditis
top5.rationale: EBV-triggered immune-mediated cerebellar syndrome fits the ataxia, dysmetria, dysarthria, and hypometric saccades, with the ear findings as a separate or incidental process.

top5.diagnosis: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) triggered by EBV
top5.rationale: Monophasic post-infectious demyelinating syndrome can present with encephalopathy, cerebellar signs, and CSF lymphocytosis, though the normal MRI makes it less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Bacterial meningitis or otogenic intracranial complication (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae) from right otomastoiditis
top5.rationale: Ear infection with perforation and recent myringotomy could seed the CNS; however, the indolent course, clear CSF, and lack of meningeal signs argue against this.

top5.diagnosis: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (paraneoplastic or post-infectious)
top5.rationale: Cerebellar ataxia with saccadic abnormalities and myoclonus-like features could fit, but the absence of opsoclonus and the clear EBV context make it less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Primary CNS lymphoma
top5.rationale: Partially enhancing, nodular, leptomeningeal-spreading mass with normal spectroscopy and perfusion can be seen in lymphoma, which often lacks the marked choline elevation or hyperperfusion of glioblastoma; the indolent course and CSF dissemination fit.

top5.diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis
top5.rationale: Leptomeningeal nodules along the brainstem and temporal lobe with insular/basal ganglia FLAIR changes fit sarcoid, and the absence of systemic symptoms does not exclude isolated CNS disease; normal spectroscopy/perfusion supports a non-neoplastic granulomatous process.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis with tuberculoma
top5.rationale: Leptomeningeal enhancement along the basal cisterns and brainstem is classic for TB meningitis, and tuberculomas can appear as enhancing parenchymal masses; the patient's African-American/Caribbean ancestry raises risk, though no travel or systemic symptoms are reported.

top5.diagnosis: Low-grade glioma (e.g., ganglioglioma or pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma) with leptomeningeal spread
top5.rationale: A slowly growing temporal lobe tumor can cause olfactory hallucinations and paresthesias, and normal spectroscopy/perfusion is more typical of low-grade tumors; however, leptomeningeal dissemination at presentation is unusual and argues against this.

top5.diagnosis: Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis with underlying occult malignancy (e.g., testicular germ cell tumor)
top5.rationale: Olfactory hallucinations and paresthesias could reflect limbic/basal ganglia involvement, and the enhancing mass might be an incidental companion finding; however, the nodular leptomeningeal pattern and normal CSF findings (if any) make this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with septic shock, DIC, and purpura fulminans
top5.rationale: Dog bite in an asplenic-appearing patient (small spleen with granulomas) with alcohol abuse, rapid DIC, purpura fulminans, and multi-organ failure fits this organism better than the leading hypothesis, and the dog exposure is the key overlooked clue.

top5.diagnosis: Pasteurella multocida sepsis with septic shock and DIC
top5.rationale: Also a dog-bite pathogen causing rapidly progressive sepsis, DIC, and purpura fulminans, though less classically associated with asplenia and more with local wound infection.

top5.diagnosis: Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (Streptococcus pyogenes) from a minor skin wound
top5.rationale: Explains the rapidly progressive shock, rash, multi-organ failure, and DIC, but the dog bite and asplenia point more toward a zoonotic gram-negative pathogen.

top5.diagnosis: Alcohol withdrawal with delirium tremens complicated by aspiration pneumonia and sepsis
top5.rationale: The patient stopped drinking 3 days before admission, and the confusion, agitation, and autonomic instability could be withdrawal, but this does not explain the purpura fulminans, DIC, and multi-organ failure.

top5.diagnosis: Systemic capillary leak syndrome triggered by infection
top5.rationale: Explains the hemoconcentration, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and shock, but the purpura, DIC, and dog bite suggest an infectious cause rather than idiopathic capillary leak.

top5.diagnosis: Epstein-Barr virus encephalitis with cerebellitis and possible rhombencephalitis
top5.rationale: CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose/protein, preceding EBV mononucleosis, and MRI showing only mastoid/middle-ear opacification without brain parenchymal abnormality fit post-infectious or direct EBV CNS invasion causing ataxia, dysarthria, and cognitive changes.

top5.diagnosis: Acute cerebellitis (post-infectious, likely viral) complicating otitis media/mastoiditis
top5.rationale: Prominent truncal ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and hypometric saccades with normal brain MRI and CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis strongly localize to cerebellum, a classic post-infectious phenomenon after EBV or other viral illness.

top5.diagnosis: Skull base osteomyelitis (otogenic) with intracranial extension
top5.rationale: Persistent right otalgia, perforated tympanic membrane, bloody purulent ear canal, and mastoid/middle-ear opacification despite antibiotics raise concern for temporal bone osteomyelitis, though intact tegmen and no bony destruction on CT make this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebellar stroke or venous sinus thrombosis
top5.rationale: Acute onset of ataxia, dysarthria, and imbalance could suggest posterior circulation ischemia or venous infarction, but normal non-contrast MRI, MR venogram, and lack of vascular risk factors make this unlikely.

top5.diagnosis: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (e.g., anti-Yo, anti-Hu) or autoimmune cerebellitis
top5.rationale: Subacute cerebellar syndrome with cognitive changes and weight loss could reflect a paraneoplastic or autoimmune process, though no cancer history and acute post-EBV timeline make it less probable.

top5.diagnosis: Epstein–Barr virus encephalitis with cerebellitis and brainstem involvement
top5.rationale: EBV is the established infection; direct CNS invasion or post-infectious immune-mediated cerebellitis/brainstem encephalitis explains the ataxia, dysarthria, saccadic abnormalities, and cognitive changes, with CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and atypical lymphocytes as clues.

top5.diagnosis: Post-infectious cerebellitis (EBV-triggered autoimmune/paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration)
top5.rationale: A post-infectious autoimmune process targeting cerebellar and brainstem antigens can produce the subacute pancerebellar syndrome with truncal ataxia, dysmetria, and dysarthria despite normal MRI, with CSF lymphocytosis and oligoclonal bands as supportive clues.

top5.diagnosis: Skull base osteomyelitis (malignant otitis externa) with intracranial extension and meningoencephalitis
top5.rationale: Progressive otalgia, tympanic perforation, bloody otorrhea, and mastoid/middle-ear opacification despite antibiotics suggest invasive infection of the temporal bone/skull base, with possible direct CNS spread producing the neurologic findings; elevated alkaline phosphatase and ESR/CRP would support this.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with secondary cerebellar/brainstem venous infarction
top5.rationale: Otomastoiditis can cause septic or aseptic dural sinus thrombosis; although MRV reportedly showed normal flow, the constellation of ataxia, dysarthria, and cognitive changes could reflect venous congestion or small-vessel thrombosis not evident on routine imaging.

top5.diagnosis: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (occult malignancy, e.g., Hodgkin lymphoma) triggered by EBV
top5.rationale: EBV is associated with Hodgkin lymphoma and other malignancies; a paraneoplastic antibody-mediated cerebellar syndrome could explain the progressive pancerebellar signs, weight loss, and lymphadenopathy, with CSF pleocytosis and normal MRI as clues.

top5.diagnosis: Epstein–Barr virus encephalitis with cerebellitis and cranial neuropathy (post-infectious/parainfectious)
top5.rationale: The antecedent heterophile-positive mononucleosis, persistent adenopathy, and cerebellar/executive findings fit direct CNS EBV involvement or post-infectious cerebellitis better than a bacterial process, and the CSF lacks pleocytosis despite a normal glucose/protein profile.

top5.diagnosis: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) triggered by EBV
top5.rationale: A monophasic post-infectious demyelinating syndrome 2–4 weeks after EBV can explain ataxia, dysarthria, cognitive changes, and brainstem/cerebellar signs with normal initial non-contrast MRI and bland CSF.

top5.diagnosis: Skull-base osteomyelitis / malignant otitis externa with intracranial extension (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa)
top5.rationale: The perforated tympanic membrane, bloody otorrhea, mastoid opacification, and progressive cranial nerve/cerebellar dysfunction could reflect indolent skull-base infection despite intact bone on CT and lack of fever.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis complicating otomastoiditis
top5.rationale: Otogenic infection can seed the sigmoid/transverse sinus, producing cerebellar and cognitive symptoms; the MR venogram reportedly showed normal flow, but non-contrast studies can miss early or partial thrombosis.

top5.diagnosis: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome / paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (occult neoplasm, e.g., Hodgkin lymphoma)
top5.rationale: The subacute pancerebellar syndrome with dysmetria, overshoot, and truncal ataxia in a young adult, plus weight loss and lymphadenopathy, raises a paraneoplastic or autoimmune cerebellar process that could be overlooked if EBV is assumed to be the sole cause.

top5.diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke in the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) territory (lateral medullary/Wallenberg syndrome)
top5.rationale: Positional vertigo, vomiting, left-beating nystagmus, left facial sensory loss, leftward tilt, and right-sided hyperreflexia localize to the left dorsolateral medulla; vascular risk factors and stepwise worsening support stroke over peripheral vertigo.

top5.diagnosis: Vertebral artery dissection with posterior circulation ischemia
top5.rationale: A young-at-heart 69-year-old with abrupt posterior circulation symptoms and positional provocation may have an occult vertebral dissection, a diagnosis easily overlooked if only peripheral vestibular causes are considered.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebellar infarction (left posterior inferior cerebellar artery territory)
top5.rationale: Severe positional vertigo, vomiting, gait instability, and inability to tandem walk can reflect cerebellar stroke even without limb ataxia; CT is insensitive early, so MRI is discriminating.

top5.diagnosis: Vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis
top5.rationale: Acute prolonged vertigo with nausea and vomiting is classic, but the left facial sensory deficit, direction-changing nystagmus, and right-sided hyperreflexia argue against a purely peripheral cause.

top5.diagnosis: Paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) with incidental extraaxial calcified lesion
top5.rationale: The positional trigger and prior self-limited positional vertigo fit BPPV, and the parafalcine calcified lesion is likely an incidental meningioma; however, central signs make this the least unifying explanation.

top5.diagnosis: Epstein–Barr virus encephalitis/cerebellitis
top5.rationale: Recent heterophile-positive EBV mononucleosis in a college student with fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytosis, and now cerebellar/executive dysfunction fits EBV CNS invasion, which can occur without meningismus or CSF pleocytosis.

top5.diagnosis: Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis with mastoiditis/otogenic intracranial extension
top5.rationale: Right otitis media progressed to tympanic perforation, mastoid opacification, and cerebellar signs; prior antibiotics may have partially treated CSF, and pneumococcus is the leading otogenic pathogen.

top5.diagnosis: Fusobacterium necrophorum otomastoiditis with intracranial extension
top5.rationale: Adolescent with persistent otalgia, bloody otorrhea, mastoid effusion, and progressive ataxia despite beta-lactams; Fusobacterium is a classic hidden otogenic pathogen in young patients and can spread intracranially.

top5.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus encephalitis
top5.rationale: Viral prodrome followed by encephalopathy with anomia, impaired verbal fluency, perseveration, and cerebellar signs; MRI can be normal early, and CSF may lack pleocytosis.

top5.diagnosis: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) or steroid-related cerebellar syndrome
top5.rationale: Recent prednisone and hypertension-free but steroid exposure can cause cerebellar/executive dysfunction and reversible imaging findings; another specialist might overlook this medication-related complication.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebellar infarction (PICA territory) with pseudo-vestibular presentation
top5.rationale: Acute vertigo, vomiting, truncal lateropulsion, gaze-evoked nystagmus, and saccadic pursuit from posterior inferior cerebellar artery ischemia; CT is often falsely reassuring in the first 24-48 hours, and the delayed visual return and leftward tilt fit a cerebellar/brainstem localization.

top5.diagnosis: Vertebral artery dissection with posterior circulation ischemia
top5.rationale: A vascular mechanism producing acute vertigo, headache, facial paresthesias, and brainstem/cerebellar signs; dissection is a classic overlooked cause of posterior circulation stroke in older adults, and the positional onset and progressive course fit an evolving thromboembolic process.

top5.diagnosis: Vestibular migraine (with brainstem aura)
top5.rationale: Recurrent positional vertigo, headache, facial tingling, and visual lag can reflect migrainous brainstem dysfunction; the prior episode of positional vertigo and lack of focal motor findings support this, though acute onset and vascular risk factors make stroke more likely.

top5.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus reactivation causing vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis
top5.rationale: History of recurrent localized HSV and acute vertigo with nausea could reflect viral vestibular ganglionitis; however, the left facial sensory change and gaze abnormalities point more centrally, making this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Parafalcine meningioma (incidental) with unrelated acute vestibular syndrome
top5.rationale: The calcified extraaxial lesion is a classic incidental meningioma; it does not explain the acute vertigo, but it is a striking companion finding that could distract from the true posterior circulation event.

top5.diagnosis: Vertebral artery dissection (left) with posterior circulation ischemia
top5.rationale: Left-handed man with acute positional vertigo, left facial sensory changes, leftward tilt, and delayed visual return suggests lateral medullary/brainstem ischemia; dissection is a hidden risk in this demographic and can be missed on non-contrast CT.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebellar infarction (left posterior inferior cerebellar artery territory)
top5.rationale: Acute dizziness, vomiting, gait instability, and nystagmus fit cerebellar stroke; normal non-contrast CT early does not exclude ischemia, and vascular risk factors (HTN, HLD, daily wine) elevate risk.

top5.diagnosis: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) due to small vessel disease
top5.rationale: Constellation of vertigo, nausea, left facial sensory loss, nystagmus, and gait ataxia localizes to the lateral medulla; hypertension and diabetes-range glucose are hidden risk factors for small vessel occlusion.

top5.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus vestibular labyrinthitis (reactivation)
top5.rationale: History of recurrent localized HSV and acute vestibular symptoms with nausea/vomiting could reflect viral labyrinthitis; epidemiologically plausible but less likely given brainstem signs.

top5.diagnosis: Parafalcine meningioma (incidental) with unrelated acute vestibular event
top5.rationale: Extraaxial calcified lesion is likely incidental; however, in a patient with new neurologic symptoms, mass effect or seizure could be overlooked, though imaging shows no mass effect.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebellar infarction (left posterior inferior cerebellar artery territory), likely due to vertebral artery dissection
top5.rationale: Acute persistent vertigo, vomiting, leftward tilt, left-beating nystagmus, saccadic pursuit, and truncal ataxia point to a central vestibular lesion; normal early CT is expected in acute posterior-circulation stroke, and the delayed visual return/positional worsening can reflect cerebellar/brainstem involvement.

top5.diagnosis: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from vertebral artery dissection
top5.rationale: Left facial tingling over the malar/jaw region with decreased pinprick suggests trigeminal involvement, and the combination of vertigo, nausea, nystagmus, gait ataxia, and leftward tilt fits a lateral medullary syndrome; the relatively preserved strength and lack of dysphagia do not exclude it.

top5.diagnosis: Vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis
top5.rationale: Acute prolonged vertigo with nausea and vomiting and no hearing loss is the classic peripheral pattern, but direction-changing/positional nystagmus, central-appearing pursuit, and truncal lateropulsion make this less likely from an imaging/lab standpoint.

top5.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus encephalitis or reactivation-related vestibular neuritis
top5.rationale: The history of recurrent localized HSV and the facial sensory symptoms could suggest viral reactivation; however, the absence of fever, encephalopathy, and CSF data makes this less likely, though it is a treatable consideration if MRI/CSF show temporal or brainstem inflammation.

top5.diagnosis: Incidental left parafalcine calcified extraaxial lesion (e.g., meningioma or calcified granuloma)
top5.rationale: The 9×16×6 mm calcified parafalcine lesion is an incidental imaging finding without mass effect or edema and does not explain the acute vertigo, but it should be noted and followed as a companion finding.

top5.diagnosis: Hodgkin lymphoma
top5.rationale: Painless bulky inguinal/iliac lymphadenopathy with necrosis, B symptoms, and preserved CD4 count on ART fits HIV-associated lymphoma, with Hodgkin as the best unifying explanation for the whole presentation.

top5.diagnosis: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)
top5.rationale: Also strongly fits HIV-associated lymphadenopathy with B symptoms and nodal necrosis, though less classic than Hodgkin for this pattern.

top5.diagnosis: Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae)
top5.rationale: 22-year cat exposure with litter handling and regional inguinal lymphadenopathy could explain the nodal findings, though systemic B symptoms and bulky iliac involvement are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous lymphadenitis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
top5.rationale: HIV infection with prior mycobacterial disease and necrotic lymph nodes supports TB reactivation, but the absence of pulmonary findings and the subacute course make it less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic Kaposi sarcoma
top5.rationale: Prior Kaposi sarcoma and HIV infection raise recurrence risk, but isolated inguinal/iliac adenopathy without cutaneous lesions is an uncommon presentation.

top5.diagnosis: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency / posterior circulation TIA from large-artery atherosclerosis (e.g., vertebral or basilar artery stenosis)
top5.rationale: Explains acute vertigo, vomiting, gait tilt, nystagmus, and crossed facial sensory symptoms better than a purely peripheral cause, and the vascular risk profile (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, age) supports it; the normal non-contrast CT does not exclude it.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebellar infarction (e.g., PICA territory) with associated brainstem signs
top5.rationale: Could account for sustained vertigo, vomiting, truncal instability, and nystagmus; the delayed visual return and crossed sensory findings suggest brainstem involvement, and CT is insensitive early.

top5.diagnosis: Vestibular migraine / migraine with brainstem aura
top5.rationale: Can produce recurrent positional vertigo, nausea, visual lag, facial paresthesias, and headache without focal infarction; prior positional vertigo and depression history may predispose, and symptoms fluctuating with head movement fit.

top5.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus reactivation causing vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis or brainstem encephalitis
top5.rationale: History of recurrent localized HSV and valacyclovir use raises the possibility of viral reactivation; could explain acute vestibular symptoms and facial sensory changes, though systemic symptoms are absent.

top5.diagnosis: Paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) plus incidental extraaxial calcified lesion (e.g., meningioma)
top5.rationale: The positional trigger and prior similar episode fit BPPV; the left parafalcine calcified lesion is likely an incidental companion finding, but this does not fully explain the persistent gait tilt, nystagmus, or crossed sensory deficits.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection
top5.rationale: CD4 count 250 with prior MAC and constitutional symptoms; CT shows necrotic iliac/inguinal nodes with soft-tissue stranding, and hepatosplenomegaly fits disseminated mycobacterial disease.

top5.diagnosis: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)
top5.rationale: Bulky, necrotic left inguinal/external iliac lymphadenopathy with hepatomegaly and B symptoms in long-standing HIV is classic for AIDS-related lymphoma.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous lymphadenitis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
top5.rationale: Necrotic inguinal and iliac nodes with fever, night sweats, and hepatosplenomegaly; TB remains a top cause of necrotic adenopathy in HIV, even with CD4 250.

top5.diagnosis: Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease) lymphadenitis
top5.rationale: 22-year cat exposure with changing litter, bulky tender inguinal nodes and fever; Bartonella can cause necrotic adenopathy and is easily overlooked in HIV.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic Kaposi sarcoma
top5.rationale: Prior KS and HIV; inguinal lymphadenopathy with soft-tissue stranding and hepatomegaly could reflect KS involvement, though nodal necrosis is atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) lymphadenitis, reactivation or immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)
top5.rationale: Prior pulmonary MAC, CD4 250 on ART, bulky necrotic inguinal/iliac nodes, fever/night sweats, and cat exposure fit atypical mycobacterial adenitis in an HIV patient.

top5.diagnosis: Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease) lymphadenitis
top5.rationale: 22-year cat, litter-changing exposure without recalled scratch, and regional necrotic inguinal lymphadenopathy with fever make bartonellosis a classic hidden zoonosis.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous lymphadenitis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
top5.rationale: HIV with prior mycobacterial disease, constitutional symptoms, and bulky necrotic inguinal/iliac nodes; travel and possible latent reactivation support TB despite negative prior RPRs.

top5.diagnosis: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (including Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus–associated lymphoma)
top5.rationale: Long-standing HIV, prior Kaposi sarcoma, CD4 250, hepatosplenomegaly, and bulky necrotic lymphadenopathy raise risk of HIV-associated lymphoma.

top5.diagnosis: Inguinal hernia with incarcerated/strangulated omentum or bowel causing reactive lymphadenopathy
top5.rationale: Known bilateral inguinal hernias, left-sided enlargement, and CT fat-containing hernias with soft-tissue stranding could explain pain and reactive nodes, though systemic symptoms point beyond a simple hernia.

top5.diagnosis: High-grade B-cell lymphoma (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) involving inguinal/iliac lymph nodes
top5.rationale: HIV with prior Kaposi's sarcoma, bulky necrotic lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, and hepatosplenomegaly fit HIV-associated lymphoma; histology would show sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells with high Ki-67 and clonal IGH rearrangement.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous lymphadenitis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) with inguinal/iliac adenopathy
top5.rationale: Necrotic bulky nodes, fevers/night sweats, prior mycobacterial disease, and HIV immunosuppression fit TB; hallmark is caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli and positive IGRA/PCR.

top5.diagnosis: Nontuberculous mycobacterial lymphadenitis (e.g., Mycobacterium avium complex) reactivation
top5.rationale: Prior pulmonary MAC and CD4 count 250 create risk for disseminated/multifocal NTM disease; histology shows poorly formed granulomas with AFB, and cultures/PCR identify the organism.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic Kaposi sarcoma involving inguinal lymph nodes
top5.rationale: Prior KS and HIV are risk factors; nodal KS can cause bulky adenopathy and necrosis, with histologic spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and HHV-8 positivity.

top5.diagnosis: Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease) lymphadenitis
top5.rationale: Cat exposure with litter changes, tender inguinal nodes, and necrosis fit bartonella; histology shows stellate necrotizing granulomas, and serology/PCR for B. henselae confirm.

top5.diagnosis: Necrotic lymphadenopathy due to disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection, with inguinal hernias as incidental
top5.rationale: Prior MAC and CD4 250 with bulky necrotic iliac/inguinal nodes fits reactivation or IRIS-like MAC, explaining fever, night sweats, and adenopathy without requiring a new pathogen.

top5.diagnosis: Bacterial lymphadenitis/abscess (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus species) arising within or adjacent to the left inguinal hernia
top5.rationale: Tender necrotic inguinal nodes with overlying soft-tissue stranding and fever could reflect a bacterial adenitis/abscess complicating a hernia, a common diagnosis that may be overlooked when HIV dominates the differential.

top5.diagnosis: Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) from the 22-year-old cat
top5.rationale: Chronic cat exposure with regional necrotic inguinal/iliac lymphadenopathy and fever fits Bartonella, though lack of recalled scratch and systemic nodes are minor contradictions.

top5.diagnosis: Lymphoma (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or Hodgkin lymphoma) involving iliac and inguinal nodes, with hepatosplenomegaly
top5.rationale: Bulky necrotic lymphadenopathy plus hepatomegaly and splenic enlargement in long-standing HIV raises lymphoma, but the subacute febrile course and prior opportunistic infections make it less parsimonious than infection.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous lymphadenitis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) with inguinal/iliac adenopathy
top5.rationale: Necrotic nodes, fever, night sweats, and HIV are compatible with TB, though no pulmonary symptoms, negative prior TB risk history, and prior MAC treatment make it less likely than MAC reactivation.

top5.diagnosis: Celiac disease (adult-onset, seronegative)
top5.rationale: Chronic diarrhea with steatorrhea (stool fat 37%), weight loss, small-bowel wall thickening/dilatation on CT, and negative tTG/EMA/IgA despite Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry and family history of GI cancer; seronegative celiac is well described and would unify the malabsorptive picture.

top5.diagnosis: Tropical sprue
top5.rationale: Travel to the Middle East followed by prolonged watery diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and small-bowel mucosal injury fits this malabsorptive disorder; partial response to antibiotics and no response to metronidazole alone is compatible.

top5.diagnosis: Whipple's disease (Tropheryma whipplei)
top5.rationale: Middle East travel, chronic diarrhea with steatorrhea, weight loss, small-bowel wall thickening, and an enlarged retroperitoneal node could reflect this culture-negative infection; it is often overlooked when stool studies are negative.

top5.diagnosis: Giardiasis (chronic, stool-PCR–negative)
top5.rationale: Travel-associated watery diarrhea, bloating, and malabsorption with repeatedly negative stool ova/parasite exams is classic for chronic giardiasis, which can be missed on routine microscopy and may partially respond to antibiotics.

top5.diagnosis: Eosinophilic gastroenteritis
top5.rationale: Chronic relapsing diarrhea, vomiting, weight loss, and small-bowel thickening with a normal peripheral eosinophil count can occur; it would explain the steroid-responsive or antibiotic-partial courses and is easily overlooked without mucosal eosinophil quantification.

top5.diagnosis: Celiac disease (adult-onset, seronegative)
top5.rationale: Chronic diarrhea with steatorrhea (stool fat 37%), weight loss, and small-bowel wall thickening/dilatation on CT fit malabsorption; negative serology does not exclude seronegative celiac, especially with Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry and family history of GI cancer.

top5.diagnosis: Whipple's disease (Tropheryma whipplei infection)
top5.rationale: Middle-aged man with chronic watery diarrhea, weight loss, malabsorption, and enlarged retroperitoneal node; CT small-bowel thickening and negative routine stool studies are classic for this culture-negative intracellular pathogen.

top5.diagnosis: Immunoproliferative small intestinal disease (IPSID) / Mediterranean lymphoma
top5.rationale: Travel to Middle East, chronic diarrhea, malabsorption, weight loss, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy suggest this alpha-heavy-chain disease variant; may be overlooked without small-bowel biopsy and serum protein electrophoresis.

top5.diagnosis: Tropical sprue
top5.rationale: History of travel to Middle East followed by chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, and malabsorption; partial response to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole supports this diagnosis, though usually responds more completely.

top5.diagnosis: Neuroendocrine tumor (e.g., gastrinoma or VIPoma)
top5.rationale: Refractory secretory diarrhea, hypokalemia (stool potassium 21.7 mmol/L), metabolic acidosis (CO2 30.3), and normal upper endoscopy except esophagitis; CT node and ground-glass lung nodule could represent metastatic disease, and omeprazole may mask gastrinoma.

top5.diagnosis: Celiac disease (complicated/refractory, seronegative)
top5.rationale: Chronic diarrhea with steatorrhea (stool fat 37%), weight loss, small-bowel wall thickening/dilatation, and negative tTG/EMA/IgA despite Ashkenazi ancestry; seronegativity can occur with selective IgA deficiency or refractory sprue, and the duodenal erosions/ulcerations fit an enteropathy.

top5.diagnosis: Whipple's disease (Tropheryma whipplei)
top5.rationale: Middle-aged man with chronic watery diarrhea, malabsorption, weight loss, arthralgias/adenopathy (retroperitoneal node), and small-bowel involvement; PAS-positive macrophages on duodenal biopsy are the hallmark, and it can mimic seronegative sprue.

top5.diagnosis: Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) with chronic giardiasis or malabsorption
top5.rationale: Recurrent diarrheal illnesses, small-bowel thickening, and possible immunoglobulin abnormalities; CVID predisposes to giardiasis and sprue-like enteropathy, and stool parasite testing can be falsely negative.

top5.diagnosis: Tropical sprue
top5.rationale: Travel to the Middle East followed by chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and small-bowel mucosal injury; responds to antibiotics (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole gave partial improvement), and biopsy shows villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia.

top5.diagnosis: Neuroendocrine tumor (e.g., gastrinoma/ VIPoma) with secondary malabsorption
top5.rationale: Chronic secretory diarrhea, hypokalemia (stool K 21.7), metabolic acidosis, and small-bowel wall thickening; a retroperitoneal node and family history of stomach cancer raise concern for a hormone-secreting tumor, though the steatorrhea and biopsy findings would be atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy)
top5.rationale: Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, chronic diarrhea with steatorrhea (stool fat 37%), weight loss, and duodenal/antral erosions; serology may be falsely negative on a gluten-containing diet or with IgA deficiency, and the striking esophageal inlet patch/Barrett's is an incidental companion finding.

top5.diagnosis: Tropical sprue
top5.rationale: Travel to the Middle East followed by chronic watery diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, and small-bowel wall thickening/dilatation on CT; symptoms partially responded to broad-spectrum antibiotics (TMP-SMX), and no other traveler was affected, consistent with an environmental enteropathy.

top5.diagnosis: Giardiasis (chronic)
top5.rationale: Travel-related exposure, chronic diarrhea with leukocytes but negative stool O&P (low sensitivity), partial response to metronidazole, and small-bowel involvement; the prior Blastocystis hominis finding may have been a red herring.

top5.diagnosis: Whipple's disease (Tropheryma whipplei)
top5.rationale: Middle-aged man with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, steatorrhea, small-bowel thickening, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy; Ashkenazi ancestry and service-industry work are not protective, and the indolent course with negative routine stool studies fits.

top5.diagnosis: Neuroendocrine tumor (e.g., gastrinoma/Zollinger-Ellison syndrome)
top5.rationale: Family history of stomach cancer, chronic erosive esophagitis/gastritis/duodenal ulcers, prominent gastric fold, and chronic diarrhea with weight loss; the ground-glass lung nodule and retroperitoneal node could represent metastatic disease, and PPIs may mask acid hypersecretion.

top5.diagnosis: Celiac disease (seronegative, presenting as chronic diarrhea with malabsorption and small-bowel wall thickening)
top5.rationale: Explains chronic diarrhea, 16-kg weight loss, stool fat 37%, small-bowel wall thickening/dilatation, and partial TMP-SMX response (some antibiotics may suppress secondary bacterial overgrowth); negative serology does not exclude celiac, especially with IgA sufficiency and patchy villous atrophy.

top5.diagnosis: Whipple's disease (Tropheryma whipplei infection)
top5.rationale: Classic cause of chronic diarrhea, weight loss, malabsorption, and small-bowel wall thickening with mesenteric adenopathy; negative routine stool studies and partial antibiotic response fit, and it is easily overlooked without PAS staining or PCR of duodenal biopsy.

top5.diagnosis: Small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) complicating chronic PPI use and prior gastrointestinal surgery/inflammation
top5.rationale: Omeprazole, chronic diarrhea, bloating, and partial response to metronidazole and TMP-SMX all support SIBO; it can produce malabsorption and fluid-filled small bowel, though it may be secondary rather than primary.

top5.diagnosis: Eosinophilic gastroenteritis
top5.rationale: Can cause chronic diarrhea, vomiting, weight loss, and small-bowel wall thickening; normal peripheral eosinophils do not exclude it, and it may respond partially to antibiotics only if there is superimposed infection or spontaneous fluctuation.

top5.diagnosis: Neuroendocrine tumor (e.g., gastrinoma or VIPoma) with secondary malabsorption
top5.rationale: Explains chronic watery diarrhea, weight loss, and small-bowel wall thickening; normal amylase/lipase and lack of flushing do not exclude it, and it may be missed if not specifically pursued with fasting gut hormone levels.

top5.diagnosis: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC)
top5.rationale: Solid enhancing renal mass with intravoxel fat and proteinuria in a smoker fits clear cell RCC, which can contain fat and present with paraneoplastic proteinuria; VHL mutation is the molecular hallmark.

top5.diagnosis: Fat-poor angiomyolipoma
top5.rationale: Renal mass with intravoxel fat is classic for AML; however, the heterogeneous solid appearance and proteinuria are atypical, and AML is usually incidental without systemic findings.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberous sclerosis complex–associated renal angiomyolipoma
top5.rationale: Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and renal fat-containing mass could suggest a TSC spectrum disorder with AMLs, though no skin or CNS findings are reported.

top5.diagnosis: Diabetic nephropathy with incidental renal mass
top5.rationale: Long-standing type 2 diabetes and stage 4 CKD with proteinuria could explain the renal dysfunction; the mass may be an incidental RCC or AML, a combination another specialist might overlook.

top5.diagnosis: IgA nephropathy with incidental renal mass
top5.rationale: Microscopic hematuria, proteinuria, and CKD could reflect IgA nephropathy; the renal mass may be incidental, and this primary glomerular disease might be overlooked amid the oncologic workup.

top5.diagnosis: Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell or papillary), right kidney, with associated proteinuria and CKD
top5.rationale: The enhancing, fat-containing solid renal mass with microscopic hematuria and proteinuria in a 72-year-old smoker is the unifying lesion; paraneoplastic or nephrotic-range proteinuria and CKD can accompany RCC.

top5.diagnosis: Fat-poor angiomyolipoma
top5.rationale: A solid renal mass with intravoxel fat on MRI is classic for AML, though the heterogeneous enhancement and proteinuria are atypical; another specialist might overlook this benign mimic.

top5.diagnosis: Diabetic nephropathy with incidental renal mass
top5.rationale: Long-standing type 2 diabetes and stage 4 CKD with proteinuria fit diabetic kidney disease, while the small renal mass may be an incidental companion finding.

top5.diagnosis: IgA nephropathy or other primary glomerulonephritis
top5.rationale: Microscopic hematuria, proteinuria, and a positive ANA raise the possibility of a glomerular process independent of the renal mass, though complement and dsDNA are normal.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberous sclerosis complex–associated renal angiomyolipoma
top5.rationale: Bilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and fat-containing renal mass could suggest a syndromic association, though no classic skin or neurologic features are described.

top5.diagnosis: Renal cell carcinoma, clear cell type
top5.rationale: Solid enhancing heterogeneous renal mass with intravoxel fat on MRI is highly suspicious for clear cell RCC, and fat content is a classic feature.

top5.diagnosis: Fat-poor angiomyolipoma
top5.rationale: Intravoxel fat within a solid renal mass can also be seen in angiomyolipoma, though less likely given the heterogeneous enhancement and patient's age.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic kidney disease due to diabetic nephropathy and hypertensive nephrosclerosis
top5.rationale: Baseline creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, proteinuria (3+ albumin), and history of diabetes and hypertension strongly suggest underlying chronic kidney disease.

top5.diagnosis: IgA nephropathy
top5.rationale: Microscopic hematuria, proteinuria, and positive ANA (though nonspecific) could indicate an immune-mediated glomerulonephritis, though no active urinary sediment.

top5.diagnosis: Renal oncocytoma
top5.rationale: A solid renal mass with heterogeneous signal and central scar-like features can mimic oncocytoma, though intravoxel fat is atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell, likely papillary or clear cell with fat)
top5.rationale: 72-year-old with 30 pack-year smoking history, Dominican Republic origin, solid enhancing renal mass with intravoxel fat and proteinuria; smoking and immigrant status raise RCC risk, and fat-containing renal masses suggest clear cell or angiomyolipoma variant.

top5.diagnosis: Fat-poor angiomyolipoma
top5.rationale: Intravoxel fat on MRI in a solid renal mass can indicate angiomyolipoma; however, absence of tuberous sclerosis and demographic profile make it less likely than RCC, but it is a key radiologic-pathologic mimic.

top5.diagnosis: Oncocytoma
top5.rationale: Solid renal mass with heterogeneous signal and fat in a patient with CKD and diabetes; oncocytoma can mimic RCC and is often incidental, though fat is atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Diabetic nephropathy with superimposed hypertensive nephrosclerosis
top5.rationale: Stage 4 CKD, proteinuria, diabetes, and hypertension are prominent; the renal mass may be incidental, and CKD progression could explain proteinuria and creatinine elevation.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic interstitial nephritis (possibly analgesic or medication-related)
top5.rationale: History of unknown oral medications in Dominican Republic for flank pain, now with CKD and proteinuria; prior analgesic or nephrotoxic exposure could contribute to chronic kidney disease, though less likely than diabetic/hypertensive causes.

top5.diagnosis: Acute eosinophilic leukemia (FIP1L1-PDGFRA-positive myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia)
top5.rationale: Marked leukocytosis with 83% eosinophils, splenomegaly, diffuse skeletal FDG uptake, and reactive lymph node biopsy lacking lymphoma all point to a primary eosinophilic myeloid neoplasm rather than reactive eosinophilia.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (PDGFRA-negative)
top5.rationale: A myeloproliferative eosinophilic neoplasm remains the best unifying explanation for extreme eosinophilia, splenomegaly, and marrow/skeletal uptake when reactive and PDGFRA-associated causes are excluded.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated strongyloidiasis with hyperinfection syndrome
top5.rationale: Travel to Indonesia and rural India, diarrhea, weight loss, rash, and striking eosinophilia fit helminth infection; however, negative Strongyloides serology and absence of pulmonary symptoms make it less likely than a myeloid neoplasm.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia with Loeffler-like endomyocardial involvement
top5.rationale: Eosinophilic myocarditis/endocardial fibrosis is a classic complication of sustained hypereosinophilia and could explain fatigue and exercise intolerance, though cardiac imaging is not yet reported.

top5.diagnosis: Ulcerative colitis flare with reactive eosinophilia and incidental travel-associated parasitic exposure
top5.rationale: Established ulcerative colitis could explain diarrhea and weight loss, but the degree of eosinophilia, splenomegaly, and skeletal FDG uptake are far out of proportion to a simple colitis flare.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
top5.rationale: Marked eosinophilia with eosinophilic infiltration of spleen, skeleton, and lymph nodes plus reactive marrow findings fits a myeloproliferative neoplasm; travel and UC are red herrings.

top5.diagnosis: Strongyloidiasis with hyperinfection syndrome
top5.rationale: Rural India travel, eosinophilia, diarrhea, and lymphadenopathy fit Strongyloides; however, negative serology and absence of pulmonary symptoms make it less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome)
top5.rationale: Recent rural India travel, eosinophilia, diarrhea, and rash are compatible with acute schistosomiasis, though stool ova were negative and lymphadenopathy is atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Lymphoma with eosinophilia (e.g., Hodgkin lymphoma or T-cell lymphoma)
top5.rationale: Lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and marked eosinophilia can accompany lymphoma; biopsy showed only reactive hyperplasia, but sampling error remains possible.

top5.diagnosis: Ulcerative colitis flare with reactive eosinophilia
top5.rationale: Known UC with recent diarrhea and weight loss could explain GI symptoms, but the extreme eosinophilia and systemic lymphadenopathy are disproportionate and suggest another process.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
top5.rationale: Marked leukocytosis with 83% eosinophils, splenomegaly, diffuse skeletal FDG uptake, and reactive lymph node biopsy without lymphoma suggest a primary eosinophilic myeloid neoplasm; would need marrow aspirate/biopsy with FIP1L1-PDGFRA and other fusion testing.

top5.diagnosis: Strongyloidiasis with hyperinfection syndrome
top5.rationale: Travel to Indonesia and rural India, diarrhea, weight loss, rash, and extreme eosinophilia fit Strongyloides stercoralis; negative serology does not exclude it, and stool ova/parasite exam lacks sensitivity—would need repeated stool, agar plate, or duodenal biopsy.

top5.diagnosis: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with PDGFRA rearrangement (FIP1L1-PDGFRA)
top5.rationale: A clonal eosinophilic disorder presenting with diarrhea, splenomegaly, and marked eosinophilia; lymph node showing reactive eosinophils/plasma cells is compatible, and tyrosine kinase inhibitor responsiveness makes this a critical molecular diagnosis.

top5.diagnosis: Lymphocytic variant hypereosinophilic syndrome (L-HES)
top5.rationale: Clonal or aberrant T cells can drive severe eosinophilia with skin and GI involvement; flow cytometry of blood/marrow for aberrant T-cell populations and T-cell receptor rearrangement would be key clues.

top5.diagnosis: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA/Churg-Strauss)
top5.rationale: Eosinophilia, rash, GI symptoms, and constitutional findings could fit an eosinophilic vasculitis, though asthma and pulmonary infiltrates are absent; ANCA and biopsy of affected tissue would be needed.

top5.diagnosis: Fat-poor angiomyolipoma (renal angiomyolipoma) with incidental chronic kidney disease
top5.rationale: Intravoxel fat on MRI is near-pathognomonic for AML, and the mass's small size, mixed echogenicity, and internal vascularity fit; the CKD, proteinuria, and ANA positivity may be unrelated comorbid findings, making this the strongest alternative that explains the mass without invoking malignancy.

top5.diagnosis: Papillary renal cell carcinoma, type 1 or 2
top5.rationale: A solid enhancing renal mass with heterogeneous signal and microscopic fat can be a papillary RCC, especially in a patient with CKD and hematuria; however, the absence of weight loss, anorexia, or gross hematuria and the stable 1.5-year history argue against an aggressive tumor.

top5.diagnosis: Diabetic nephropathy with incidental renal mass (e.g., oncocytoma or lipid-poor AML)
top5.rationale: Long-standing type 2 diabetes and stage 4 CKD with proteinuria and bland urinary sediment strongly suggest diabetic kidney disease as the primary renal process, while the mass may be an incidental benign or indolent lesion; this combination explains more findings (CKD, proteinuria, hypertension) with fewer contradictions than a primary renal malignancy.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (e.g., from prior unknown medications or NSAIDs) with incidental renal mass
top5.rationale: The remote flank pain treated with unknown oral medications in the Dominican Republic could represent a prior drug-induced interstitial nephritis or analgesic nephropathy contributing to CKD and proteinuria, with the mass being an incidental finding; this is often overlooked when a mass dominates the presentation.

top5.diagnosis: Renal oncocytoma
top5.rationale: Oncocytomas are benign, can be heterogeneous on MRI, may contain microscopic fat, and are often incidental; they would explain the mass without systemic symptoms, though the imaging features overlap with RCC and the CKD remains unexplained by this diagnosis alone.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
top5.rationale: Marked leukocytosis (146,700) with 83% eosinophils, diffuse skeletal FDG uptake, splenomegaly, and reactive lymph nodes fit a myeloproliferative neoplasm with eosinophilia; travel-related parasites were largely excluded.

top5.diagnosis: FIP1L1-PDGFRA-positive myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia
top5.rationale: Same hypereosinophilic picture with systemic FDG avidity and splenic involvement; a clonal eosinophilic marrow disorder that can present with diarrhea and fatigue and is not excluded by a reactive lymph-node biopsy.

top5.diagnosis: Strongyloidiasis with hyperinfection/disseminated strongyloidiasis
top5.rationale: Remote exposure in Indonesia/India, diarrhea, weight loss, rash, splenomegaly, and extreme eosinophilia fit; however, negative stool ova/parasites and negative Strongyloides serology argue against it, though serology can be falsely negative.

top5.diagnosis: Lymphoma with secondary eosinophilia (e.g., Hodgkin lymphoma or T-cell lymphoma)
top5.rationale: Enlarged mesenteric/retroperitoneal nodes, splenomegaly, and diffuse skeletal FDG uptake could reflect occult lymphoma with reactive eosinophilia; the single node biopsy showed only reactive hyperplasia, so sampling error remains possible.

top5.diagnosis: Ulcerative colitis flare with reactive hypereosinophilia
top5.rationale: Established UC on mesalamine with recurrent diarrhea and weight loss; however, the extreme eosinophil count and diffuse skeletal FDG uptake are far out of proportion to a typical UC flare and suggest an alternative or superimposed process.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
top5.rationale: Marked leukocytosis with 83% eosinophils, splenomegaly, diffuse skeletal FDG uptake, and reactive-appearing lymph node biopsy fit a myeloproliferative neoplasm better than a reactive process, and travel exposures may be a red herring.

top5.diagnosis: Acute eosinophilic leukemia / eosinophilic blast crisis
top5.rationale: Extreme eosinophilia with immature forms and marrow/skeletal involvement could represent an acute leukemic process that a single lymph node biopsy would miss.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated strongyloidiasis with hyperinfection syndrome
top5.rationale: Remote travel to Indonesia and rural India, eosinophilia, diarrhea, and weight loss fit Strongyloides; negative serology does not exclude hyperinfection, and mesalamine/possible steroid exposure could predispose.

top5.diagnosis: Filarial infection (e.g., Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia species) with tropical pulmonary eosinophilia-like syndrome
top5.rationale: Southeast Asian exposure, marked eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and rash are compatible with lymphatic filariasis, which routine stool ova/parasite testing would not detect.

top5.diagnosis: Ulcerative colitis flare with reactive eosinophilia and incidental travel-associated parasitic exposure
top5.rationale: Known UC with prior diarrhea/weight loss could explain GI symptoms, while the striking eosinophilia and lymphadenopathy may be a separate or superimposed process that the leading hypothesis may wrongly unify.

top5.diagnosis: Sarcoidosis (systemic, with splenic, hepatic, pulmonary, and nodal involvement)
top5.rationale: Unifying granulomatous disease explains night sweats, RUQ pain, splenic hypodense lesions, perilymphatic lung nodules, bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, elevated ACE, erythema nodosum history, and prior knee arthritis.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated tuberculosis (including splenic and pulmonary involvement)
top5.rationale: Night sweats, abdominal pain, splenic hypodense lesions, hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, and perilymphatic nodules are classic for miliary/disseminated TB, and prior erythema nodosum can be a primary TB manifestation.

top5.diagnosis: Lymphoma (e.g., Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin) with splenic, hepatic, and nodal involvement
top5.rationale: B symptoms, matted inguinal nodes, splenic lesions, mediastinal/hilar adenopathy, and perilymphatic lung nodules fit lymphoid malignancy, though the indolent course and erythema nodosum history are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection (e.g., Mycobacterium avium complex)
top5.rationale: Can mimic sarcoidosis with granulomatous splenic, pulmonary, and nodal disease, night sweats, and elevated ACE, especially in a host without overt immunodeficiency.

top5.diagnosis: Histoplasmosis (disseminated or pulmonary with splenic involvement)
top5.rationale: Travel to a coastal northeastern region and systemic granulomatous findings with splenic lesions, adenopathy, and night sweats could reflect endemic fungal infection, though less common than sarcoidosis or TB in this presentation.

top5.diagnosis: Sarcoidosis (systemic, with splenic, hepatic, pulmonary, and lymph-node involvement)
top5.rationale: Noncaseating granulomas can produce splenic hypodense lesions, perilymphatic lung nodules, hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, elevated ACE, erythema nodosum history, and a palpable spleen tip, all fitting a single granulomatous mechanism.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection
top5.rationale: Night sweats, abdominal pain, splenic hypodense lesions, mediastinal/hilar adenopathy, and perilymphatic nodules are classic for miliary/disseminated TB; granulomatous inflammation can also elevate ACE and cause erythema nodosum.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated histoplasmosis
top5.rationale: Exposure to a coastal northeastern region is less typical, but Histoplasma can cause splenic lesions, mediastinal adenopathy, and perilymphatic nodules; granulomatous response may mimic sarcoidosis with elevated ACE.
