top5.rationale: Pontomedullary hypoplasia, microcephaly, developmental delay, and episodic brainstem-mediated cyanosis fit a congenital pontocerebellar hypoplasia syndrome; the hyperhomocysteinemia and thrombosis could be incidental or due to a separate prothrombotic state.

top5.diagnosis: Episodic cyanosis/apnea due to laryngomalacia/bronchomalacia with reflux and central apnea, on a background of static encephalopathy
top5.rationale: Incomplete vocal-cord adduction, bronchomalacia, reflux, and agitation-triggered spells could explain the cyanotic episodes, but this is a symptomatic descriptor rather than a unifying diagnosis for the microcephaly, hypomyelination, and metabolic/thrombotic findings.

top5.diagnosis: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) deficiency with homocystinuria
top5.rationale: Markedly elevated homocysteine (159.5 μmol/L) with low methionine, low cystine, and normal B12/folate points to a remethylation defect; microcephaly, hypomyelination, pontomedullary hypoplasia, and venous sinus thrombosis are classic complications.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebral sinovenous thrombosis (sagittal/straight sinus) with secondary venous infarction
top5.rationale: MRI showed sagittal and straight sinus thrombus with engorged vein of Galen; elevated d-dimer (1570 ng/mL), prolonged PT/aPTT, and femoral vein thrombosis confirm a hypercoagulable state driving episodic cyanosis/apnea and neurologic decline.

top5.diagnosis: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia (e.g., PCH type 6/7) with hypomyelination
top5.rationale: Pontomedullary hypoplasia, diminutive corpus callosum, and hypomyelination on MRI are disproportionate to white-matter depletion and suggest a malformation component; episodic cyanosis, bradycardia, and central apnea fit brainstem dysfunction.

top5.diagnosis: Disorders of remethylation other than MTHFR deficiency (e.g., cblC/cblD defects, methionine synthase deficiency)
top5.rationale: Low methionine with elevated homocysteine and normal B12 can also occur in intracellular cobalamin defects; however, the normal amino acid profile and absence of methylmalonic aciduria make these less likely than MTHFR deficiency.

top5.diagnosis: 16p11.2 duplication–associated neurodevelopmental disorder with incidental microcephaly
top5.rationale: Array-CGH revealed 16p11.2 duplication, which can cause developmental delay and microcephaly but is often benign; it may be an incidental companion finding rather than the primary cause of the progressive neurologic and thrombotic phenotype.

top5.diagnosis: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) deficiency with homocystinuria
top5.rationale: Homocysteine 159.5 μmol/L with low methionine, normal B12/folate, microcephaly, hypomyelination, and venous thrombosis fit this treatable remethylation defect.

top5.diagnosis: Cobalamin C (cblC) defect
top5.rationale: Combined methylmalonic acidemia and homocystinuria can present with microcephaly, hypomyelination, and thrombosis; low methionine and elevated homocysteine support it.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebral sinovenous thrombosis with secondary hypoxic-ischemic injury
top5.rationale: Documented sagittal/straight sinus thrombus and femoral vein thrombosis can explain episodic cyanosis/apnea, bradycardia, and neurologic decline.

top5.diagnosis: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia (e.g., PCH type 1/2)
top5.rationale: Pontomedullary hypoplasia, microcephaly, developmental delay, and central hypoventilation-like episodes fit this genetic malformation spectrum.

top5.diagnosis: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy / ALDH7A1 deficiency
top5.rationale: Episodic cyanosis, arching, limb extension, and EEG slowing without ictal correlate may reflect a treatable metabolic epilepsy overlooked amid structural findings.

top5.diagnosis: New primary breast carcinoma (contralateral, right breast), likely invasive ductal carcinoma
top5.rationale: New rim-enhancing/spiculated 14-mm right breast mass with atypical epithelial cells and prior ER/PR+ breast cancer history; morphology favored primary over lung metastasis, and this is the most discriminating new organic finding driving the case.

top5.diagnosis: Recurrent/metastatic non-small-cell lung carcinoma to the breast
top5.rationale: Prior stage II NSCLC and TTF1/mammaglobin inconclusive staining mean lung metastasis remains a real competing explanation for the breast mass, though lower nuclear grade than prior lung tumor argues against it.

top5.diagnosis: Bipolar disorder, depressive phase, refractory, with comorbid ADHD and anxiety/agoraphobia
top5.rationale: The psychiatric presentation is the admission reason and is itself a unifying active diagnosis; ECT produced only moderate improvement, and mood symptoms may be amplified by undertreated medical illness and medication changes.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease/asthma with diffuse wheezing and tobacco use
top5.rationale: Diffuse inspiratory and expiratory wheezes plus 1–2 pack/day smoking history are a striking organic companion finding that could complicate ECT, sedation, and overall clinical stability.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic kidney disease, stage 3a (eGFR 41), possibly multifactorial
top5.rationale: Elevated BUN/creatinine and reduced eGFR are discriminating metabolic findings that may reflect hypertensive/vascular disease, medication effects, or paraneoplastic/volume issues and warrant synthesis with her oncologic and psychiatric care.

top5.diagnosis: New primary invasive breast carcinoma (contralateral, right breast)
top5.rationale: Spiculated rim-enhancing mass with atypical epithelial cells and prior ER+/PR+ breast cancer history; second primary breast cancer is the most parsimonious mechanism, with mammaglobin+/TTF1− profile expected.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic lung carcinoma to the breast
top5.rationale: Known stage II NSCLC with TTF1+ immunophenotype could seed the breast; higher nuclear grade in lung primary than breast aspirate argues against but does not exclude, and paucicellular staining was inconclusive.

top5.diagnosis: BRCA1/2-associated hereditary breast cancer syndrome
top5.rationale: Early-onset bilateral breast cancer and family history of leukemia/stomach cancer raise possibility of germline mutation driving a new primary; would explain metachronous contralateral tumor and warrants genetic testing.

top5.diagnosis: Chemotherapy/radiation-induced secondary malignancy (therapy-related breast cancer)
top5.rationale: Prior doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide and whole-breast radiation 12 years earlier could promote a new primary in the contralateral breast via mutagenic effects, though latency is long.

top5.diagnosis: Paraneoplastic depression secondary to occult malignancy
top5.rationale: Worsening refractory depression coincident with a new breast mass could reflect a paraneoplastic limbic/psychiatric syndrome; organic workup including paraneoplastic antibodies may be overlooked by psychiatry.

top5.diagnosis: Stimulant-induced psychosis (amphetamine) with delusional parasitosis and excoriations
top5.rationale: Recent 60 mg amphetamine salts, positive urine screen, and preserved insight otherwise make a substance-induced psychotic disorder the most parsimonious explanation for the fixed infestation belief, with the rash being self-induced excoriations rather than a primary dermatosis.

top5.diagnosis: Delusional parasitosis (primary monosymptomatic delusional disorder, somatic type)
top5.rationale: The encapsulated, non-bizarre fixed belief of mites with matching self-excoriations and no other psychotic features fits primary delusional parasitosis, and the psychiatric history of depression does not exclude it; the amphetamine use may be an aggravator rather than the cause.

top5.diagnosis: Porphyria cutanea tarda (HCV-associated) with secondary excoriations and possible neuropsychiatric symptoms
top5.rationale: HCV is a classic driver of PCT, which can cause photosensitive fragile skin and blistering that the patient may interpret as infestation; the low phosphorus and mildly elevated AST are unexplained by the leading psychiatric hypothesis and warrant porphyrin testing.

top5.diagnosis: Cheyletiellosis or other zoonotic mite infestation (e.g., Sarcoptes scabiei) transmitted from the child, with shared delusional infestation in the mother
top5.rationale: The child's scalp redness and the prior ED diagnosis of possible cheyletiellosis suggest a real arthropod exposure that could seed or reinforce the mother's fixed belief, and the mid-back sparing is consistent with an ectoparasite that cannot reach that area.

top5.diagnosis: Amphetamine-induced movement disorder / formication from stimulant neurotoxicity, with incidental HCV and urinary findings
top5.rationale: Stimulant use can produce tactile hallucinations of crawling even without a full delusional system, and the hematuria plus low phosphorus remain unexplained by the leading hypothesis, suggesting a broader toxic-metabolic picture.

top5.diagnosis: Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) deficiency with severe hyperhomocysteinemia and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
top5.rationale: Homocysteine 159.5 μmol/L, low methionine, normal B12/folate, and sagittal/straight sinus thrombosis with venous infarction explain the episodic cyanosis/apnea, microcephaly, hypomyelination, and pontomedullary findings better than a primary neurodegenerative or epileptic process.

top5.diagnosis: Disorders of intracellular cobalamin metabolism (e.g., cblC/cblG) with hyperhomocysteinemia and hypomethioninemia
top5.rationale: The same biochemical pattern (high homocysteine, low methionine, normal B12) can result from impaired cobalamin processing; this is a treatable mimic that also predisposes to thrombosis and white-matter disease.

top5.diagnosis: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with venous infarction/hemorrhage causing episodic apnea, cyanosis, and bradycardia
top5.rationale: The striking organic finding of sinus thrombosis may be the proximate cause of the episodic events, independent of the underlying metabolic disorder; it is an under-recognized cause of cyanotic/apneic spells in infants.

top5.diagnosis: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia (e.g., PCH type 6/7) or another primary microcephaly–pontomedullary hypoplasia syndrome
top5.rationale: Microcephaly, pontomedullary hypoplasia, corpus callosum hypoplasia, and hypomyelination fit a primary developmental malformation; the metabolic and thrombotic findings could be incidental or secondary, and this diagnosis may be overlooked if the hyperhomocysteinemia is assumed to be the sole explanation.

top5.diagnosis: 16p11.2 duplication syndrome with associated white-matter abnormalities and epilepsy/episodic autonomic dysfunction
top5.rationale: The duplication was labeled benign, but 16p11.2 copy-number variants are associated with developmental delay, microcephaly, white-matter changes, and seizures; the episodic cyanosis could reflect an epileptic or autonomic manifestation, and this diagnosis may be dismissed prematurely.

top5.diagnosis: Second primary breast carcinoma (contralateral, right breast)
top5.rationale: New spiculated rim-enhancing right breast mass 12 years after left breast cancer, with prior chest radiation and tamoxifen exposure; smoking and obesity are additional risk factors.

top5.diagnosis: Recurrent non-small-cell lung carcinoma metastatic to the breast
top5.rationale: Prior stage II NSCLC with lobectomy; TTF1/mammaglobin inconclusive on paucicellular sample, and lung is a known (though rare) source of breast metastases.

top5.diagnosis: Major depressive episode with psychotic features, refractory, in bipolar disorder
top5.rationale: Worsening depression, agoraphobia, hopelessness, and prior mania with psychotic features; psychosocial isolation and medication nonadherence are hidden drivers.

top5.diagnosis: Lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus / chronic kidney disease
top5.rationale: eGFR 41 and creatinine 1.31 in a patient with remote lithium exposure and lithium allergy/intolerance; CKD may alter psychotropic dosing and ECT risk.

top5.diagnosis: COPD/asthma exacerbation with possible superimposed respiratory infection
top5.rationale: Diffuse wheezing, 1–2 pack-day smoking history, and multiple inhalers; pulmonary comorbidity complicates ECT and may contribute to fatigue and mood symptoms.

top5.diagnosis: New primary breast carcinoma (contralateral, right breast)
top5.rationale: Rim-enhancing 14-mm mass with spiculated margins and architectural distortion on mammography/ultrasound, new since prior imaging, with cytology showing atypical epithelial cells and a lower nuclear grade than the prior lung primary—pattern favors a new primary over metastasis.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic lung carcinoma to the breast
top5.rationale: Known stage II NSCLC and TTF1/mammaglobin staining was inconclusive due to paucicellular sample; the breast lesion could represent a metastasis, though the lower nuclear grade relative to the lung primary argues against it.

top5.diagnosis: Recurrent depression/bipolar disorder as the primary reason for admission (with incidental breast mass)
top5.rationale: The admission was for refractory depression treated with ECT; the breast mass was an incidental imaging finding, and the psychiatric illness itself remains the active management problem.

top5.diagnosis: Renal insufficiency (CKD stage 3) possibly related to prior chemotherapy (doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide) or hypertension
top5.rationale: Creatinine 1.31 mg/dL with eGFR 41 mL/min/1.73 m² is the only abnormal lab; this may affect medication dosing and ECT safety, and could reflect chronic nephrotoxicity.

top5.diagnosis: Tobacco-related second primary malignancy (e.g., new lung primary or other smoking-related cancer)
top5.rationale: Heavy ongoing smoking (1–2 packs/day) with prior NSCLC and breast cancer places the patient at high risk for additional smoking-related malignancies, which could be overlooked amid the breast finding.

top5.diagnosis: Recurrent/metastatic lung carcinoma to the breast (or new primary lung cancer), not a new primary breast cancer
top5.rationale: The 'new' breast mass could be a metastasis from her known NSCLC; the inconclusive TTF1/mammaglobin staining and paucicellular sample mean the primary-vs-metastasis question is unresolved, and a lung primary would explain the mass without invoking a second new malignancy.

top5.diagnosis: Primary breast carcinoma (new contralateral primary), with the lung cancer as an incidental treated companion finding
top5.rationale: Rim-enhancing spiculated mass with atypical epithelial cells and mitoses is morphologically classic for primary breast cancer, and her prior ER/PR+ breast cancer history raises risk, though the case lacks receptor studies to confirm.

top5.diagnosis: Paraneoplastic or cancer-treatment-related depression (organic mood disorder) rather than primary refractory bipolar depression
top5.rationale: Worsening depression coincides with a new breast mass and prior lung cancer; an occult malignancy or its treatment effects could be driving the psychiatric decompensation, making ECT a symptomatic rather than definitive treatment.

top5.diagnosis: Medication-induced or metabolic encephalopathy/mood disturbance (e.g., gabapentin, quetiapine, modafinil, or renal impairment with eGFR 41)
top5.rationale: Polypharmacy plus reduced renal function could contribute to cognitive/mood changes and restlessness, and the mild creatinine elevation is otherwise unexplained by the leading cancer hypothesis.

top5.diagnosis: Occult second malignancy or metastatic disease elsewhere (e.g., recurrent breast cancer, thyroid, colon, or melanoma) presenting as the breast mass
top5.rationale: The differential for a breast mass in a patient with prior breast and lung cancer includes other primaries and metastases; without definitive immunohistochemistry, a non-breast, non-lung source remains possible and would change management.

top5.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with secondary warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia (Evans syndrome)
top5.rationale: Young woman, South American origin, prior similar episode, positive DAT with warm and cold autoantibodies, spherocytes, thrombocytopenia, and constitutional symptoms fit SLE; epidemiologic lens highlights female sex and Hispanic ancestry as risk factors.

top5.diagnosis: Parvovirus B19 infection
top5.rationale: Works with children, recent travel, and a 3-month prodrome of fatigue/malaise with anemia and thrombocytopenia; B19 can cause pure red cell aplasia and immune thrombocytopenia, and is easily overlooked without specific serology.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) infection
top5.rationale: Recurrent vesicular thigh lesions confirmed as HSV-2, with systemic symptoms and possible immune-mediated cytopenias; recent travel and occupational exposure to children increase risk, and HSV can trigger or complicate autoimmune hemolysis.

top5.diagnosis: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia with warm and cold autoantibodies (mixed-type AIHA)
top5.rationale: Positive DAT with both warm and cold reacting autoantibodies, spherocytes, polychromasia, and dark urine; may be primary or secondary, and the mixed nature explains transfusion incompatibility and refractoriness.

top5.diagnosis: Leptospirosis
top5.rationale: Travel to Central America and the Caribbean, possible exposure to contaminated water or animals; can present with fever, jaundice, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypotension, though the chronic 3-month course and vesicular lesions are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Evans syndrome (warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia plus immune thrombocytopenia)
top5.rationale: Positive direct antiglobulin test with spherocytes, polychromasia, and thrombocytopenia fits combined warm AIHA and ITP; the paradox of 'incompatible' transfusions with immediate burning/flushing suggests broadly reactive warm autoantibodies rather than a single alloantibody.

top5.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with secondary Evans syndrome
top5.rationale: Young woman with cytopenias, positive antiglobulin tests, and transient vesicular thigh lesions (HSV-2) could reflect immunosuppression; however, negative lupus anticoagulant and normal inflammatory markers make this less likely than primary Evans syndrome.

top5.diagnosis: Parvovirus B19-associated pure red cell aplasia with immune thrombocytopenia
top5.rationale: Recent travel, work with children, and biphasic illness with anemia and thrombocytopenia could fit parvovirus, but the prominent spherocytes and positive Coombs test argue against pure red cell aplasia and toward hemolysis.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated herpes simplex virus type 2 infection with immune-mediated cytopenias
top5.rationale: Recurrent vesicular thigh lesions confirmed as HSV-2, weight loss, and cytopenias could indicate disseminated HSV triggering secondary immune hemolysis and thrombocytopenia, though blood cultures are sterile and no visceral lesions are described.

top5.diagnosis: Tick-borne illness (e.g., babesiosis or ehrlichiosis) with secondary immune hemolytic anemia
top5.rationale: Travel to Central America and the Caribbean and exposure to children could suggest vector-borne infection; however, normal white cell morphology, absence of schistocytes, and positive Coombs test make a direct infectious hemolysis less likely than an immune-mediated process.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis with tuberculoma (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
top5.rationale: Subacute headache, vomiting, diplopia, meningismus, basal-cistern leptomeningeal enhancement, sterile CSF, Southeast Asian origin, and a new necrotic ring-enhancing frontal mass after steroid taper fit CNS TB despite negative sputum/skin tests.

top5.diagnosis: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system (PACNS)
top5.rationale: Multifocal leptomeningeal enhancement, cortical ischemia, sterile cultures, and progressive necrotic mass with hemorrhage could reflect granulomatous angiitis, though systemic markers are normal.

top5.diagnosis: CNS lymphoma (primary or secondary)
top5.rationale: Steroid-responsive leptomeningeal process with negative initial cytology and later necrotic ring-enhancing mass can be seen with lymphoma, especially after dexamethasone exposure.

top5.diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis
top5.rationale: Basal leptomeningeal enhancement, cranial neuropathies, optic disk blurring, and negative infectious workup fit sarcoid, though no systemic findings and normal ACE are less typical.

top5.diagnosis: CNS nocardiosis or other atypical bacterial/fungal meningoencephalitis
top5.rationale: Refractory meningoencephalitis with sterile cultures and a necrotic mass could reflect an indolent opportunistic pathogen, though no clear immunodeficiency is documented.

top5.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia (Evans syndrome)
top5.rationale: The positive direct antiglobulin test with both warm and cold autoantibodies, spherocytes, thrombocytopenia, and a prior similar episode fit SLE/Evans syndrome better than a primary hematologic disorder, and the vesicular thigh lesions could be HSV-2 reactivation rather than a separate disease.

top5.diagnosis: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH) due to Donath-Landsteiner antibody
top5.rationale: Dark urine, anemia, positive DAT, and both warm- and cold-reacting autoantibodies suggest a biphasic hemolysin; PCH can cause severe intravascular hemolysis and is often overlooked when warm autoantibodies dominate the serology.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated herpes simplex virus type 2 infection with secondary immune-mediated cytopenias
top5.rationale: Recurrent vesicular thigh lesions, HSV-2 isolated from the lesion, and systemic symptoms could indicate disseminated HSV driving immune dysregulation, though the absence of fever or organ-specific findings makes this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS) with Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia
top5.rationale: The negative lupus anticoagulant does not exclude APS; however, the absence of thrombosis and the predominantly hemolytic picture make APS a weaker alternative.

top5.diagnosis: Undiagnosed inherited red-cell membrane defect (e.g., hereditary spherocytosis) with a superimposed immune hemolytic process
top5.rationale: Spherocytes and a positive DAT could reflect a primary membrane defect plus an acquired autoantibody, but the normal red-cell indexes and lack of family history argue against this being the sole explanation.

top5.diagnosis: Evans syndrome (primary autoimmune hemolytic anemia with immune thrombocytopenia)
top5.rationale: Warm and cold autoantibodies with positive DAT, spherocytes, thrombocytopenia, and no schistocytes fit combined autoimmune cytopenias; mechanism is autoantibody-mediated RBC and platelet destruction, though refractoriness to steroids and transfusion reactions suggest a broader immune dysregulation.

top5.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with secondary Evans syndrome and antiphospholipid antibodies
top5.rationale: Young woman with autoimmune cytopenias, transient visual symptoms, vesicular lesions (HSV-2 reactivation), and prior similar episode; SLE can drive warm/cold autoantibodies, and negative lupus anticoagulant does not exclude antiphospholipid syndrome or underlying connective-tissue disease.

top5.diagnosis: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (Donath-Landsteiner antibody) causing mixed autoimmune hemolysis
top5.rationale: Cold-reacting autoantibodies, dark urine, spherocytes, and positive DAT with both warm and cold reactivity; biphasic hemolysin can cause intravascular hemolysis and may be missed if only warm autoantibody is considered, especially after viral triggers like HSV.

top5.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus type 2–associated immune dysregulation with secondary autoimmune hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia
top5.rationale: Recurrent vesicular thigh lesions confirmed as HSV-2, with systemic symptoms and autoimmune cytopenias; HSV can trigger cold agglutinins and immune-mediated cytopenias, and the temporal association supports a pathogen-driven mechanism.

top5.diagnosis: Underlying lymphoproliferative disorder (e.g., indolent lymphoma or Castleman disease) causing autoimmune cytopenias
top5.rationale: Weight loss, prior spontaneous resolution of a similar illness, and refractory autoimmune hemolysis/thrombocytopenia raise concern for an occult B-cell or plasma-cell disorder producing autoantibodies; normal CT and protein electrophoresis do not fully exclude early or nodal disease.

top5.diagnosis: Evans syndrome (primary autoimmune hemolytic anemia with immune thrombocytopenia), with warm and cold autoantibodies
top5.rationale: The combination of Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia (spherocytes, polychromasia, indirect hyperbilirubinemia/urobilinogen) and thrombocytopenia with bruising, in a patient without schistocytes or microangiopathy, is the most parsimonious unifying explanation; the positive DAT with both warm and cold autoantibodies and refractoriness to steroids fits an aggressive autoimmune cytopenia.

top5.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with secondary Evans syndrome / autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia
top5.rationale: A young woman with a prior similar self-limited illness, cytopenias, transient vesicular skin lesions, visual symptoms, and a strongly positive DAT could have SLE as the underlying systemic autoimmune driver; the negative lupus anticoagulant does not exclude SLE, and this is a diagnosis a hematologist focused on the cytopenia might overlook.

top5.diagnosis: Parvovirus B19 or other viral-triggered autoimmune hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia
top5.rationale: A preceding viral-like illness with fatigue and malaise, recent travel, and a self-limited prior episode 3 years earlier suggest an infectious trigger for the autoimmune cytopenias; however, the absence of reticulocytopenia and the positive DAT make pure parvovirus aplastic crisis less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Antiphospholipid syndrome or other thrombotic microangiopathy (e.g., atypical HUS) with Coombs-positive hemolysis
top5.rationale: Thrombocytopenia, anemia, headache, visual symptoms, and hypotension could suggest a thrombotic microangiopathy, but the absence of schistocytes, normal renal function, and a positive DAT argue strongly against TTP/HUS; this is included mainly because the visual and neurologic symptoms could mislead toward a microangiopathic process.

top5.diagnosis: Disseminated herpes simplex virus type 2 infection with secondary immune cytopenias
top5.rationale: The recurrent vesicular thigh lesions confirmed as HSV-2 and the recent travel raise the possibility of a disseminated viral infection driving immune-mediated cytopenias; however, blood cultures are sterile, the lesions are localized, and HSV-2 is more likely an incidental companion finding than the unifying diagnosis.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis with tuberculoma (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
top5.rationale: Basal leptomeningeal enhancement, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose, Southeast Asian origin, and a necrotic ring-enhancing frontal mass after steroid taper fit CNS TB; negative AFB cultures and QuantiFERON do not exclude it.

top5.diagnosis: Primary CNS lymphoma
top5.rationale: Subacute meningoencephalitis with cranial neuropathies, diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement, sterile CSF, and a new necrotic periventricular frontal mass in an immunocompetent young adult; negative flow cytometry can miss parenchymal lymphoma.

top5.diagnosis: Neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium)
top5.rationale: Southeast Asian refugee exposure, leptomeningeal fibrosis, hydrocephalus requiring shunt, and a later ring-enhancing necrotic mass with susceptibility artifact fit degenerating cysticerci; serology and CSF antigen testing are often overlooked.

top5.diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis
top5.rationale: Chronic basal leptomeningitis with cranial nerve palsies, optic nerve enhancement, hydrocephalus, and a necrotic enhancing mass can occur; ANA positivity and leptomeningeal fibrosis are compatible, though systemic involvement is absent.

top5.diagnosis: CNS aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus)
top5.rationale: Steroid exposure, sputum yeast, and a necrotic ring-enhancing mass with hemorrhage/neovascularity suggest angioinvasive fungal infection; serum galactomannan and CSF fungal PCR are key but often not sent.

top5.diagnosis: Anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease
top5.rationale: Classic heliotrope/Gottron rash with proximal weakness, normal-ish CK late, and rapidly progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure with diffuse air-space disease and pneumomediastinum-like soft tissue stranding points to MDA5+ DM with RP-ILD, a hallmark of this autoantibody.

top5.diagnosis: Classic dermatomyositis with secondary aspiration pneumonia and sepsis
top5.rationale: The initial violaceous rash, proximal muscle weakness, elevated CK, and muscle biopsy showing perivascular inflammation/myonecrosis fit classic DM; respiratory failure could be from aspiration and superimposed infection, though the progressive course favors a primary lung process.

top5.diagnosis: Clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis with interstitial lung disease
top5.rationale: Prominent cutaneous findings with relatively preserved or improving CK after steroids, but severe respiratory failure out of proportion to muscle disease, fits CADM-ILD spectrum often associated with MDA5.

top5.diagnosis: Antisynthetase syndrome
top5.rationale: Myositis with interstitial lung disease and skin changes can occur, but the absence of mechanic's hands, arthritis, and the specific heliotrope/Gottron papules make this less likely than DM; still a consideration in inflammatory myopathy with lung involvement.

top5.diagnosis: Paraneoplastic dermatomyositis
top5.rationale: DM can be a paraneoplastic manifestation, and the patient's age and severe course warrant malignancy search; however, extensive workup including bone marrow and GI biopsies showed no malignancy, making this less likely but not fully excluded.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis with tuberculoma (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
top5.rationale: Basal cistern leptomeningeal enhancement, communicating hydrocephalus requiring shunt, sterile CSF cultures, negative IGRA/TST, and a later necrotic ring-enhancing mass with restricted diffusion rim fit CNS TB paradoxically worsening on therapy (IRIS/undertreated).

top5.diagnosis: Primary CNS lymphoma
top5.rationale: Sterile CSF, leptomeningeal enhancement, and a new necrotic ring-enhancing periventricular/frontal mass with restricted diffusion rim in an immunocompetent young man; flow cytometry and cytology can be falsely negative, especially with steroids.

top5.diagnosis: CNS aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus)
top5.rationale: Sputum grew yeast, brief amphotericin stopped for rash, and progressive necrotic ring-enhancing mass with hemorrhage/susceptibility and leptomeningeal spread fit angioinvasive fungal disease; serum galactomannan/BAL fungal studies not reported.

top5.diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis
top5.rationale: Leptomeningeal enhancement, cranial neuropathies (bilateral abducens, facial), optic disk edema, and positive ANA with normal IgG can mimic TB; necrotic mass is atypical but possible with coalescent granulomas.

top5.diagnosis: Nocardia brain abscess (Nocardia asteroides complex)
top5.rationale: Subacute meningoencephalitis with sterile cultures, sputum yeast contaminant, and a necrotic ring-enhancing mass with restricted diffusion rim; partially treated with TMP-SMX later, and Nocardia can be missed on routine CSF and bacterial cultures.

top5.diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism (likely with right ventricular strain and thrombocytopenia from platelet consumption)
top5.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, hypoxemia, syncope, calf cramping, recent 4-hour flight, D-dimer >10,000, incomplete RBBB with diffuse ST/T changes, and thrombocytopenia all point to venous thromboembolism with clot burden and platelet consumption.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension with acute decompensation
top5.rationale: Recurrent or organized thromboemboli can cause exertional syncope, hypoxemia, RV strain pattern, and modest thrombocytopenia, though the acute presentation favors fresh PE.

top5.diagnosis: Paradoxical embolism via patent foramen ovale causing pulmonary embolism and transient neurologic symptoms
top5.rationale: A PFO could permit clot passage, but the dominant findings are pulmonary; this would be overlooked if no shunt evaluation is performed.

top5.diagnosis: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis (HIT) as a unifying mechanism
top5.rationale: Thrombocytopenia with thrombosis could explain PE and low platelets, but the patient had no prior heparin exposure, making this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Occult malignancy with hypercoagulable state and tumor-related thrombocytopenia
top5.rationale: Unexplained thrombocytopenia and massive D-dimer elevation could reflect malignancy-associated thrombosis, though no cancer history or systemic symptoms are present.

top5.diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism (likely with right heart strain and thrombocytopenia)
top5.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, profound hypoxemia, syncope, recent 4-hour flight, elevated D-dimer >10,000, incomplete RBBB with diffuse ST-T changes, and thrombocytopenia all point to a unifying thromboembolic event with right ventricular strain.

top5.diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism complicated by paradoxical embolism and cryptogenic stroke (e.g., via patent foramen ovale)
top5.rationale: Syncope with hypoxemia could reflect PE plus paradoxical embolization; the family history of stroke at 58 and diffuse ECG changes might otherwise be overlooked as incidental.

top5.diagnosis: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) with thrombosis
top5.rationale: Thrombocytopenia (120,000) with a prothrombotic presentation could reflect HIT if she had recent heparin exposure, though no medications are reported—an overlooked possibility if she received heparin before transfer.

top5.diagnosis: Occult malignancy (e.g., mucinous adenocarcinoma) with Trousseau syndrome and pulmonary embolism
top5.rationale: Unexplained thrombocytopenia and massive thromboembolism in a 60-year-old could signal an occult malignancy-associated hypercoagulable state, which a specialist might overlook without imaging.

top5.diagnosis: Antiphospholipid syndrome with pulmonary embolism and thrombocytopenia
top5.rationale: A unifying autoimmune thrombophilia could explain PE, thrombocytopenia, and family history of stroke, though it is less likely without prior thrombotic events or pregnancy morbidity.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
top5.rationale: Southeast Asian refugee-camp birth with BCG vaccination, military service in the Middle East, basal-cistern leptomeningeal enhancement, sterile CSF/brain cultures, and transient response to anti-TB therapy all fit TB meningitis despite negative TST/IGRA and smears.

top5.diagnosis: CNS nocardiosis (Nocardia species)
top5.rationale: Subacute meningoencephalitis with leptomeningeal fibrosis, negative routine cultures, and progression to a necrotic ring-enhancing mass despite broad antibiotics is classic for partially treated Nocardia, an exposure-linked diagnosis easily missed without modified acid-fast staining.

top5.diagnosis: CNS aspergillosis (Aspergillus species)
top5.rationale: Refugee-camp and military exposures, sputum yeast, serous otitis media, and a necrotic hemorrhagic frontal mass with leptomeningeal spread fit angioinvasive Aspergillus, which can be culture-negative and unresponsive to standard antibacterials.

top5.diagnosis: Primary CNS lymphoma (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma)
top5.rationale: A 29-year-old with 3 weeks of headache/vomiting, leptomeningeal enhancement, sterile CSF, and a new necrotic periventricular mass could have occult immunosuppression or EBV-driven lymphoma despite negative flow cytometry on a single CSF sample.

top5.diagnosis: Neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium)
top5.rationale: Southeast Asian origin and prior ivermectin exposure raise the possibility of a parasitic CNS infection presenting with basilar meningitis and a later necrotic/granulomatous mass, though the absence of typical scolex or calcifications makes it less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis with tuberculoma (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
top5.rationale: Basal leptomeningeal enhancement, hydrocephalus, sterile CSF, Southeast Asian origin, and a new necrotic ring-enhancing mass despite partially active anti-TB therapy fit TB best, though negative sputum/skin tests and lack of microbiologic confirmation are contradictions.

top5.diagnosis: Primary CNS lymphoma
top5.rationale: Sterile leptomeningeal inflammation, cranial neuropathies, progressive necrotic mass, and negative flow cytometry can occur with leptomeningeal lymphoma, but the acute febrile course, diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement, and initial response to antimicrobials are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis
top5.rationale: Leptomeningeal enhancement, cranial nerve palsies, optic disk edema, and a necrotic mass could reflect sarcoid, but the absence of pulmonary findings, normal ACE (not reported), and negative systemic workup make it less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Fungal meningitis with cerebral abscess (e.g., Cryptococcus or Aspergillus)
top5.rationale: Refugee camp exposure, serous otitis, and partially treated meningoencephalitis with a necrotic mass could fit an indolent fungal infection, but sterile cultures, lack of immunodeficiency, and negative fungal studies argue against it.

top5.diagnosis: Autoimmune/paraneoplastic meningoencephalitis with secondary tumefactive demyelination
top5.rationale: Positive ANA, steroid responsiveness, and sterile leptomeningeal inflammation could suggest an autoimmune process, but the necrotic mass, marked basal enhancement, and lack of systemic autoimmune features make this the least likely alternative.

top5.diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism
top5.rationale: Hypoxemia with syncope, D-dimer >10,000, incomplete RBBB with diffuse ST/T changes, recent 4-hour flight, and transient calf cramping all point to venous thromboembolism with right-heart strain.

top5.diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism with paradoxical embolism causing syncope
top5.rationale: The combination of PE physiology and syncope could reflect a right-to-left shunt (e.g., patent foramen ovale) with transient cerebral embolism, explaining the dramatic but rapidly resolving event.

top5.diagnosis: Deep vein thrombosis with early pulmonary embolism
top5.rationale: The transient left calf cramping plus marked D-dimer elevation supports a peripheral thrombotic source, even though leg symptoms resolved.

top5.diagnosis: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)
top5.rationale: Platelet count of 120,000 is a striking unexplained finding; if the patient received heparin during the workup, HIT could complicate thrombosis, though this is less likely without prior heparin exposure.

top5.diagnosis: Occult malignancy with hypercoagulable state (e.g., pancreatic or lung cancer)
top5.rationale: Unexplained thrombocytopenia, massive D-dimer elevation, and unprovoked VTE in a 60-year-old could signal an underlying malignancy, a diagnosis easily overlooked when the acute PE dominates the picture.

top5.diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism
top5.rationale: Recent 4-hour flight, obesity, syncope with severe hypoxemia, calf cramping, and D-dimer >10,000 make venous thromboembolism the dominant exposure-driven risk.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
top5.rationale: Retired health care worker with prior travel-related VTE risk may have recurrent silent emboli causing exertional syncope and hypoxemia with incomplete RBBB.

top5.diagnosis: Fat embolism syndrome
top5.rationale: Occult long-bone fracture or recent procedure in a health care worker could explain sudden hypoxemia, syncope, thrombocytopenia, and calf pain without chest pain.

top5.diagnosis: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
top5.rationale: Platelet count of 120,000 with recent hospitalization or occupational heparin exposure could cause paradoxical thrombosis and PE, though no prior heparin is documented.

top5.diagnosis: Pneumothorax
top5.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, hypoxemia, and syncope in an obese patient could reflect spontaneous pneumothorax, though calf pain and D-dimer elevation favor VTE.

top5.diagnosis: Eosinophilic myocarditis with cardioembolic stroke (Löffler endocarditis / hypereosinophilic syndrome)
top5.rationale: The combination of marked eosinophilia (16%), apical akinesis with aneurysmal change, and diffuse smooth endocardial echodense deposits causing multiple bihemispheric infarcts in a pregnant woman is most parsimoniously explained by eosinophilic endomyocardial disease with thrombus and embolization.

top5.diagnosis: Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) with apical aneurysm and cardioembolic stroke
top5.rationale: A Guatemala-born patient with an apical akinetic/aneurysmal right ventricular apex and multiple embolic strokes fits Chagas cardiomyopathy, which can present with apical aneurysm and thrombus even without classic risk factors; endocardial deposits could represent thrombus.

top5.diagnosis: Antiphospholipid syndrome with Libman–Sacks endocarditis and embolic strokes
top5.rationale: Pregnancy, prior stillbirth, thrombocytopenia trend, and endocardial deposits with systemic emboli suggest APS; however, anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant were negative, lowering likelihood.

top5.diagnosis: Infective endocarditis (e.g., Streptococcus viridans or enterococcal) with septic emboli
top5.rationale: Fever, urinary mixed bacteria, and multiple small infarcts could reflect embolic events, but the absence of valvular vegetations, negative cultures, and the diffuse endocardial pattern make this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Eclampsia / posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) with atypical infarcts
top5.rationale: Headache, visual symptoms, and pregnancy suggest eclampsia/PRES, but the MRI pattern of multiple small acute infarcts and the echocardiographic endocardial findings are not typical, making it a secondary consideration.

top5.diagnosis: Libman-Sacks endocarditis with systemic embolism (antiphospholipid syndrome)
top5.rationale: Echocardiography shows diffuse endocardial deposits with normal valves and no wall-motion abnormality, and multiple small infarcts in multiple vascular territories plus thrombocytopenia and pregnancy fit APLS with sterile emboli.

top5.diagnosis: Infective endocarditis (e.g., Streptococcus viridans or enterococcal) with septic emboli
top5.rationale: Fever, leukocytosis, elevated CRP, and multiple acute infarcts in different territories suggest embolic showers, though the smooth diffuse endocardial material and negative cultures make this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Cardiac amyloidosis with endocardial thrombus and embolic stroke
top5.rationale: Diffuse endocardial echodensity distinct from myocardium, hyperkinetic ventricle with obliteration, and systemic emboli could reflect amyloid deposition with secondary thrombosis, though no heart failure or low voltage is described.

top5.diagnosis: Eosinophilic myocarditis (e.g., hypersensitivity or parasitic) with mural thrombus
top5.rationale: Marked eosinophilia (16%) and endocardial deposits with embolic infarcts fit eosinophilic endomyocardial disease, though the absence of fever and normal ventricular function make it less typical.

top5.diagnosis: Chagas disease with apical aneurysm and embolic stroke
top5.rationale: Right ventricular apical akinesis/aneurysm and endocardial thrombus are classic for Chagas cardiomyopathy, and the patient immigrated from Guatemala; however, the left-sided hyperkinesis and diffuse endocardial material are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Acute pulmonary embolism (provoked by recent 4-hour flight; possibly with paradoxical embolism)
top5.rationale: The leading hypothesis fits the hypoxemia, syncope, calf cramping, D-dimer >10,000, and RV strain pattern, but it leaves the thrombocytopenia unexplained and does not account for the diffuse ST depressions/T-wave inversions as well as an alternative.

top5.diagnosis: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis (HIT) presenting as pulmonary embolism
top5.rationale: A specialist may overlook HIT because she reports no medications, but recent hospitalization or heparin exposure could be hidden; thrombocytopenia plus thrombosis explains more findings than PE alone, though the acute presentation without prior heparin is a contradiction.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) with acute decompensation
top5.rationale: The incomplete RBBB, hypoxemia, syncope, and recent travel fit CTEPH, and it could explain why she desaturated so profoundly; however, the normal NT-proBNP and absence of prior symptoms argue against chronic disease.

top5.diagnosis: Fat embolism syndrome or amniotic fluid embolism (unlikely given no trauma/pregnancy)
top5.rationale: These can cause sudden hypoxemia, syncope, and thrombocytopenia, but there is no supporting history; included because the thrombocytopenia is otherwise unexplained and a specialist might anchor on PE.

top5.diagnosis: Incidental pulmonary embolism with an alternative cause of syncope (e.g., arrhythmia or vasovagal)
top5.rationale: The striking organic finding of PE may be an incidental companion finding; the syncope could be vasovagal or arrhythmic, and the thrombocytopenia may be separate, explaining more findings with fewer contradictions than PE alone.

top5.diagnosis: Antiphospholipid syndrome with Libman-Sacks endocarditis and embolic strokes
top5.rationale: Multifocal infarcts, endocardial deposits, and pregnancy loss history fit APS despite negative anticardiolipin and β2-glycoprotein antibodies, which can be falsely negative in pregnancy.

top5.diagnosis: Infective endocarditis (e.g., Streptococcus gallolyticus or oral streptococci) with septic emboli
top5.rationale: Remote dental or urinary source, fever 11 days prior, mixed urine bacteria, and endocardial material suggest culture-negative or partially treated endocarditis causing embolic strokes.

top5.diagnosis: Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) with apical aneurysm and cardioembolic stroke
top5.rationale: Guatemalan birth and travel, right ventricular apical aneurysm, and endocardial thrombus are classic for Chagas cardiomyopathy, a diagnosis easily overlooked in non-endemic settings.

top5.diagnosis: Peripartum cardiomyopathy with left ventricular thrombus and embolic strokes
top5.rationale: Third-trimester pregnancy, sinus tachycardia, and hyperkinetic ventricle with endocardial material could represent early peripartum cardiomyopathy with mural thrombus.

top5.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with Libman-Sacks endocarditis and neuropsychiatric manifestations
top5.rationale: Young woman with pregnancy loss, bipolar/panic history, and endocardial deposits; negative serologies do not exclude SLE, and pregnancy can modulate autoantibody titers.

top5.diagnosis: Libman-Sacks endocarditis with systemic embolism (antiphospholipid syndrome or SLE)
top5.rationale: The new endocardial deposits, multiple bihemispheric infarcts, thrombocytopenia trend, and prior pregnancy loss fit an autoimmune valvulopathy with embolic stroke better than a primary cardiac or thrombotic disorder.

top5.diagnosis: Infective endocarditis (e.g., Streptococcus viridans or Enterococcus) with septic emboli
top5.rationale: Fever, mixed urinary bacteria, elevated CRP, and multiple small infarcts could reflect culture-negative or partially treated endocarditis, and the endocardial material may be vegetation rather than sterile thrombus.

top5.diagnosis: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (marantic endocarditis) associated with occult malignancy
top5.rationale: Guatemalan-born woman with prior tuberculosis, anemia, weight-stable pregnancy, and new endocardial deposits; occult gastric or pancreatic cancer can cause NBTE and embolic strokes, explaining the findings without invoking autoimmunity.

top5.diagnosis: Eclampsia / atypical preeclampsia with posterior reversible encephalopathy and embolic phenomenon
top5.rationale: Headache, visual changes, hyperreflexia, and elevated LDH/ALT in a 33-week pregnant woman with gestational diabetes could represent preeclampsia, though the multiple embolic-appearing infarcts and endocardial deposits are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis or CNS tuberculosis with vasculitis and secondary cardiac involvement
top5.rationale: Prior positive PPD, Guatemalan origin, and headache with visual symptoms could reflect reactivation TB with basilar meningitis causing small-vessel infarcts, and endocardial tuberculosis (though rare) could explain the cardiac findings.

top5.diagnosis: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS) with Libman-Sacks endocarditis and embolic infarcts
top5.rationale: Multifocal small infarcts in multiple vascular territories, new endocardial deposits, thrombocytopenia trend, and pregnancy (a prothrombotic state) fit CAPS; negative anticardiolipin/β2GPI does not exclude it, and pregnancy can modulate serologies.

top5.diagnosis: Infective endocarditis (e.g., Streptococcus gallolyticus or HACEK organism) with septic emboli
top5.rationale: Fever, leukocytosis, elevated CRP, hematuria/albuminuria, and multiple embolic infarcts with new endocardial material suggest culture-negative or fastidious endocarditis; prior mixed urinary bacteria and dental/valvular sources may be overlooked.

top5.diagnosis: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (marantic endocarditis) associated with occult malignancy or hypercoagulable state
top5.rationale: Sessile endocardial deposits with systemic emboli and normal valves, plus elevated LDH and alkaline phosphatase, raise concern for a paraneoplastic hypercoagulable state; pregnancy-related hypercoagulability amplifies risk.

top5.diagnosis: Peripartum cardiomyopathy with left ventricular thrombus and embolic stroke
top5.rationale: Hyperkinetic ventricle with apical obliteration and endocardial echodensity could reflect thrombus in a hyperdynamic, underfilled ventricle; however, the diffuse endocardial material and right ventricular aneurysm are atypical.

top5.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with Libman-Sacks endocarditis and secondary antiphospholipid syndrome
top5.rationale: Young woman with pregnancy, thrombocytopenia, proteinuria, and endocardial deposits; negative ANA/anti-dsDNA not reported, but seronegative or incomplete lupus with secondary APS can present with embolic phenomena.

top5.diagnosis: Invasive fungal sinusitis/rhinosinusitis (e.g., Mucorales such as Rhizopus or Aspergillus) with oropharyngeal extension
top5.rationale: Immunosuppressed (prednisone, methotrexate, infliximab) diabetic with chronic necrotizing ulcerated tonsillar/pharyngeal mass, black/gray exudate, and no response to antibiotics; endemic fungi or molds fit the subacute indolent course and vascular invasion.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) of the oropharynx/head and neck
top5.rationale: South American birth, chronic 7-week ulcerative tonsillar/pharyngeal lesion with weight loss and adenopathy, negative PPD in an immunosuppressed host; another specialist might overlook TB given the negative skin test and lack of pulmonary symptoms.

top5.diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil/oropharynx
top5.rationale: 78-year-old with a firm, ulcerated tonsillar mass extending to the pharyngeal wall and aryepiglottic fold, ipsilateral adenopathy, weight loss, and no response to antimicrobials; malignancy can be indolent and masked by immunosuppression.

top5.diagnosis: Lymphoma (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) of the tonsil/head and neck
top5.rationale: Chronic immunosuppression (methotrexate, anti-TNF, prednisone) increases lymphoma risk; firm tonsillar mass with regional nodes and B symptoms (weight loss, weakness) can mimic infection and may be overlooked.

top5.diagnosis: Endemic fungal infection (e.g., Histoplasma, Blastomyces, or Coccidioides) or atypical mycobacterial infection (e.g., Mycobacterium avium complex)
top5.rationale: South American origin and rural New England gardening exposure raise concern for endemic mycoses or atypical mycobacteria causing chronic ulcerative pharyngitis in an immunosuppressed host; these are easily missed when routine bacterial cultures are negative.

top5.diagnosis: Invasive fungal sinusitis/oropharyngeal mucormycosis (e.g., Rhizopus, Mucor) or Aspergillus, in the setting of chronic immunosuppression (prednisone, methotrexate, infliximab) and poorly controlled diabetes
top5.rationale: Chronic indolent ulcerative tonsillar/pharyngeal mass with progressive local invasion despite antibiotics, in a diabetic on TNF-α inhibitor and steroids, fits angioinvasive hyphal infection with tissue necrosis and negative bacterial cultures.

top5.diagnosis: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (or other EBV-driven lymphoproliferative disorder)
top5.rationale: Chronic ulcerating midline/upper aerodigestive mass with systemic symptoms (weight loss, anemia, elevated ESR/CRP) in an immunosuppressed patient; EBV-driven lymphoproliferation is a hallmark mechanism with TNF-α inhibitor and methotrexate exposure.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculosis (or atypical mycobacterial infection, e.g., M. avium complex) of the oropharynx/head and neck
top5.rationale: Indolent ulcerative tonsillar lesion with cervical adenopathy, weight loss, anemia, and elevated inflammatory markers in a patient on anti-TNF-α therapy; negative PPD does not exclude reactivation TB in immunosuppressed hosts.

top5.diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil/oropharynx (HPV-associated or conventional)
top5.rationale: Persistent firm tonsillar mass with ulceration, otalgia-like throat pain, weight loss, and asymmetric cervical lymphadenopathy in an older patient; chronic ulceration can mimic infection, and immunosuppression may accelerate oncogenesis.

top5.diagnosis: Endemic fungal infection (e.g., Paracoccidioidomycosis, Histoplasmosis) reactivated from prior South American residence
top5.rationale: Born in South America with remote travel, chronic ulcerative oropharyngeal lesions, and immunosuppression could allow reactivation of endemic dimorphic fungi; mucosal ulceration and cervical adenopathy are classic, and this is easily overlooked without specific exposure history.

top5.diagnosis: Invasive fungal sinusitis/rhinosinusitis (e.g., Aspergillus or Mucorales) with tonsillar/oropharyngeal extension
top5.rationale: Chronic immunosuppression (prednisone, methotrexate, infliximab), diabetes, and a progressive necrotic ulcerated tonsillar/pharyngeal mass unresponsive to antibiotics strongly suggest an angioinvasive fungal infection, even without classic sinus symptoms.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), extrapulmonary/oropharyngeal
top5.rationale: Born in South America with remote travel, chronic progressive ulcerated tonsillar lesion, weight loss, and immunosuppression increase risk; negative PPD and lack of classic pulmonary symptoms do not exclude extrapulmonary TB.

top5.diagnosis: Non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection (e.g., Mycobacterium avium complex)
top5.rationale: Immunosuppressed host with chronic ulcerating pharyngeal lesion and rural New England gardening exposure; NTM can cause indolent head and neck disease and is often overlooked without specific cultures.

top5.diagnosis: Endemic fungal infection (e.g., Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides) with oropharyngeal involvement
top5.rationale: South American birth and rural New England gardening exposure provide geographic risk for dimorphic fungi; chronic ulcerated mucosal lesions and immunosuppression fit, though less common than invasive mold.

top5.diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil/oropharynx
top5.rationale: Progressive firm tonsillar mass, ulceration, weight loss, and neck adenopathy in an elderly patient; immunosuppression and chronic inflammation may increase risk, and malignancy can mimic infection.

top5.diagnosis: Sézary syndrome (erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma)
top5.rationale: Chronic erythroderma with madarosis, ectropion, palmoplantar keratoderma, alopecia, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, markedly elevated IgE, and a CD4:CD8 ratio of 10 with CD3+CD7− cells despite initially sparse Sézary cells.

top5.diagnosis: Atopic dermatitis with secondary erythroderma and staphylococcal colonization/infection
top5.rationale: Eczematous/interface dermatitis on biopsy, extreme IgE elevation, eosinophilia, lichenification, and recurrent MSSA skin infections fit an allergic/atopic diathesis, though the CD4:CD8 skew and CD7 loss argue for CTCL.

top5.diagnosis: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) / drug-induced pseudolymphoma
top5.rationale: Erythroderma with eosinophilia, urticaria, and lymphadenopathy temporally linked to antibiotics (cephaloridine, TMP-SMX, nafcillin) could explain flares, but persistence for 18 months off drugs makes this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL)
top5.rationale: Generalized lymphadenopathy, erythroderma, eosinophilia, hyper-IgE, and recurrent infections may occur in AITL, but absence of clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement and lack of systemic B symptoms/autoimmune features make it less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Hypereosinophilic syndrome / eosinophilic dermatitis
top5.rationale: Marked peripheral eosinophilia (up to 20%) with erythroderma and pruritus could reflect a primary eosinophilic disorder, but the CD4:CD8 ratio of 10 and CD7− T cells point to a malignant T-cell clone rather than idiopathic hypereosinophilia.

top5.diagnosis: Chronic invasive fungal sinusitis/rhinosinusitis (e.g., Aspergillus or Mucorales) with tonsillar and pharyngeal extension
top5.rationale: Immunosuppression (prednisone, methotrexate, infliximab, diabetes) plus progressive ulceration, gray exudate, and deep tissue invasion despite antibiotics fits angioinvasive fungal infection; cultures for bacteria were negative and no fever is typical.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) of the tonsil and pharynx
top5.rationale: Chronic odynophagia, ulcerated tonsillar mass, weight loss, and cervical adenopathy in an immunosuppressed patient from South America; negative PPD does not exclude active TB, and standard throat cultures miss mycobacteria.

top5.diagnosis: Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection (e.g., Mycobacterium avium complex) of the head and neck
top5.rationale: Indolent ulcerating tonsillar/pharyngeal lesion with regional adenopathy in an immunosuppressed host on anti-TNF therapy; NTM are not detected on routine bacterial cultures and can mimic malignancy or fungal disease.

top5.diagnosis: Lymphoma (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) involving the tonsil and pharynx
top5.rationale: Persistent firm tonsillar mass with ulceration, weight loss, and asymmetric cervical lymphadenopathy in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis on immunosuppressants; chronic inflammation and immunosuppression increase lymphoma risk, and the lack of response to antibiotics or steroids is concerning.

top5.diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil/pharynx
top5.rationale: A nonhealing ulcerated tonsillar mass with extension to the pharyngeal wall and aryepiglottic fold, weight loss, and firm consistency in an older patient; no smoking history does not exclude HPV-related or other head and neck cancer, and the indolent course with negative bacterial cultures warrants biopsy.

top5.diagnosis: Invasive fungal sinusitis/rhinosinusitis (e.g., Aspergillus or Mucorales) with tonsillar/pharyngeal extension
top5.rationale: Immunosuppressed (prednisone, methotrexate, infliximab) with diabetes; chronic ulcerative tonsillar/pharyngeal mass unresponsive to antibiotics, negative bacterial cultures, and CT showing enhancing soft-tissue thickening with hazy-margin nodes fits angioinvasive fungal infection.

top5.diagnosis: Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), extrapulmonary/head-and-neck
top5.rationale: Born in South America, chronic 7-week ulcerative tonsillar lesion with cervical adenopathy, negative PPD (anergy from immunosuppression), and no fever; CT nodal asymmetry with hazy margins is compatible with necrotizing granulomatous adenitis.

top5.diagnosis: Squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil/oropharynx
top5.rationale: Elderly patient with a firm, ulcerated tonsillar mass extending to pharyngeal wall and aryepiglottic fold, weight loss, and asymmetric enhancing neck nodes with irregular hazy margins on CT; no smoking history does not exclude HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer.

top5.diagnosis: Lymphoma (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) of the tonsil
top5.rationale: Chronic non-healing tonsillar mass with progressive ulceration, systemic symptoms (weight loss, weakness), anemia, elevated ESR/CRP, and immunosuppression (methotrexate, anti-TNF) predisposing to lymphoproliferative disease; CT shows enhancing soft-tissue mass and prominent nodes.

top5.diagnosis: Endemic mycosis (e.g., Histoplasma capsulatum or Blastomyces dermatitidis) presenting as chronic ulcerative pharyngotonsillitis
top5.rationale: South American origin and rural New England garden exposure; chronic ulcerative mucosal lesions with cervical adenopathy and negative bacterial cultures in an immunosuppressed host fit endemic fungal infection, though less common than TB or malignancy.

top5.diagnosis: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (HTLV-1-associated)
top5.rationale: Born in Puerto Rico (HTLV-1-endemic), chronic erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, CD4:CD8 ratio 10 with CD3+CD7- cells, and Sézary-like cells despite negative HTLV-1 serology (serology can be falsely negative in ATLL).

top5.diagnosis: Sézary syndrome (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma)
top5.rationale: Erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, alopecia, palmoplantar keratoderma, CD4:CD8 ratio 10, and CD7-negative T cells; flow cytometry may miss low blood tumor burden.

top5.diagnosis: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) / severe cutaneous adverse reaction
top5.rationale: Eosinophilia (20%), urticaria after TMP-SMX, erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and transaminitis; may have been triggered by cephaloridine or sulfonamide and persist.

top5.diagnosis: Strongyloidiasis with hyperinfection syndrome
top5.rationale: Puerto Rico origin, eosinophilia, erythroderma, and prior prednisone; Strongyloides IgG can be falsely negative in hyperinfection, and larvae can cause diffuse rash and sepsis.

top5.diagnosis: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL)
top5.rationale: Erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and possible autoimmune features; can present with urticaria and be missed on limited flow cytometry.

top5.diagnosis: Sézary syndrome (erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma)
top5.rationale: Chronic erythroderma with pruritus, alopecia, madarosis, ectropion, palmoplantar keratoderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, marked peripheral eosinophilia, elevated IgE (26,260 IU/L), elevated LDH (425 U/L), and a CD4:CD8 ratio of 10 with CD3+CD7− cells on flow cytometry are classic; the 'few possible Sézary cells' and nondiagnostic skin/lymph node biopsies reflect the well-known sampling pitfall in erythrodermic CTCL.

top5.diagnosis: Atopic dermatitis with secondary erythroderma (eczematous erythroderma)
top5.rationale: Eczematous and interface dermatitis on biopsy, extreme IgE elevation, eosinophilia, and pruritus fit a severe atopic diathesis; however, the CD4:CD8 ratio of 10 and CD7− population are atypical and raise concern for evolving CTCL.

top5.diagnosis: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) / drug-induced erythroderma with eosinophilia
top5.rationale: Temporal association with trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, urticaria, peripheral eosinophilia (20%), fever, lymphadenopathy, and elevated LDH fit DRESS; the process may have been triggered or perpetuated by multiple antibiotics and the underlying erythroderma.

top5.diagnosis: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL)
top5.rationale: Erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, elevated IgE, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia-like features can occur; however, the absence of clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement and lack of B symptoms/autoimmune phenomena make this less likely.

top5.diagnosis: Hypereosinophilic syndrome / eosinophilic dermatitis (including parasitic or idiopathic)
top5.rationale: Marked eosinophilia (up to 20%, absolute 1330/mm³) with erythroderma and elevated IgE could reflect a hypereosinophilic process; Strongyloides and other parasite serologies were negative, but a trial of antiparasitic therapy or bone marrow evaluation might be warranted if CTCL workup remains negative.

top5.diagnosis: Sézary syndrome (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, leukemic variant)
top5.rationale: Erythroderma with madarosis, ectropion, palmoplantar keratoderma, CD4:CD8 ratio of 10 with CD3+CD7− cells, and rare Sézary cells on smear fit despite negative TCR clonality.

top5.diagnosis: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL)
top5.rationale: Erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, high IgE, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia-like features can mimic CTCL but may be overlooked without nodal architecture review.

top5.diagnosis: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) / drug-induced pseudolymphoma
top5.rationale: Eosinophilia, urticaria after TMP-SMX, erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and elevated IgE suggest a severe cutaneous adverse reaction, though chronicity and CD7− T cells argue against a simple drug eruption.

top5.diagnosis: Hypereosinophilic syndrome / eosinophilic dermatitis
top5.rationale: Persistent absolute eosinophilia (up to 1330/mm³), IgE of 26,260 IU/L, and eczematous/interface dermatitis could represent a primary eosinophilic disorder with cutaneous and nodal involvement.

top5.diagnosis: Strongyloidiasis (occult parasitic infection) with reactive erythroderma and eosinophilia
top5.rationale: Born in Puerto Rico, eosinophilia, urticaria, and erythroderma warrant consideration of Strongyloides despite negative IgG, as immunosuppression can cause false-negative serology and hyperinfection.

top5.diagnosis: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL)
top5.rationale: Erythroderma, madarosis, ectropion, CD4:CD8 ratio of 10 with CD3+CD7− cells, hypercalcemia-like features absent but HTLV-1 testing may be falsely negative in early disease; Puerto Rican origin fits HTLV-1 endemicity.

top5.diagnosis: Sézary syndrome (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma)
top5.rationale: Exfoliative erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, alopecia, palmoplantar keratoderma, and rare Sézary cells; negative TCR clonality and flow cytometry do not exclude early or patch-stage disease.

top5.diagnosis: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) / severe cutaneous adverse reaction
top5.rationale: Eosinophilia, urticaria after TMP-SMX, erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and hepatic involvement; may persist or evolve into autoimmune sequelae even after drug withdrawal.

top5.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with psoriasiform dermatitis
top5.rationale: Family history of SLE, positive ANA at 1:40 speckled, erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, and cytopenias; skin biopsy interface dermatitis supports lupus, though dsDNA negative.

top5.diagnosis: Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL)
top5.rationale: Erythroderma, generalized lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, hypergammaglobulinemia (IgE elevated), and constitutional symptoms; may lack TCR clonality in early stages and can mimic drug hypersensitivity.

top5.diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke due to embolic occlusion of the right middle cerebral artery (M1/M2)
top5.rationale: Hyperdense right MCA clot on CT, corresponding CTA filling defect, and a classic right-hemisphere syndrome (left hemiparesis, gaze preference, anosagnosia, dysarthria) with a small lenticulostriate infarct core and salvageable penumbra make this the unifying diagnosis.

top5.diagnosis: Cardioembolic stroke from occult paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
top5.rationale: Large proximal MCA embolus with no detected large-artery source is most often cardioembolic; paroxysmal AF is the most common occult mechanism and would be missed without prolonged rhythm monitoring.

top5.diagnosis: Large-artery atherosclerotic stroke from an unstable ipsilateral carotid or intracranial plaque
top5.rationale: Age, hypercholesterolemia, and remote smoking history support an atherothrombotic/artery-to-artery embolic source, though no significant stenosis was documented.

top5.diagnosis: Transient ischemic attack preceding the completed stroke (crescendo TIA)
top5.rationale: Two episodes of transient left facial numbness 2 weeks and 2 days before admission represent recurrent ischemia in the same vascular territory, marking this as a crescendo presentation rather than a single event.

top5.diagnosis: Hypercoagulable state (e.g., antiphospholipid antibody syndrome or inherited thrombophilia) contributing to thromboembolism
top5.rationale: Anticardiolipin IgG was borderline elevated and protein C/S, activated protein C resistance, and lupus anticoagulant were sent; a prothrombotic tendency is a less common but testable unifying explanation for embolic stroke without an identified source.

top5.diagnosis: Cardioembolic stroke (embolic occlusion of the right MCA) from a proximal embolic source such as atrial fibrillation, left atrial thrombus, or aortic arch atheroma
top5.rationale: Abrupt maximal-onset deficit with a visible MCA clot and no detected large-artery stenosis fits an embolic mechanism; the negative workup for a source does not exclude paroxysmal AF or aortic atheroma, and prior transient facial numbness/syncope may reflect earlier emboli.

top5.diagnosis: Large-artery atherosclerotic stroke (atherothrombotic occlusion of the right MCA) superimposed on hypercholesterolemia and family history of stroke
top5.rationale: Hypercholesterolemia plus a family history of stroke supports an atherosclerotic/thrombotic mechanism, though the absence of documented carotid or intracranial stenosis makes this less likely than embolism.

top5.diagnosis: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome with arterial thrombosis
top5.rationale: The case includes anticardiolipin IgG/IgM and lupus anticoagulant testing; a positive result would provide a unifying prothrombotic mechanism for arterial occlusion in a patient without conventional embolic source.

top5.diagnosis: Inherited thrombophilia (e.g., factor V Leiden/activated protein C resistance, protein C or S deficiency) causing arterial thrombosis
top5.rationale: An activated protein C resistance screen and protein C/S levels were sent; a positive result would identify a hypercoagulable mechanism that a stroke specialist might overlook in an older patient.

top5.diagnosis: Cervical artery dissection with secondary thromboembolism
top5.rationale: The fall and syncopal episode could reflect dissection-related symptoms; dissection is a classic cause of MCA territory embolic stroke and can be missed if imaging focuses only on the intracranial circulation.

top5.diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke due to right middle cerebral artery (M1) occlusion, cardioembolic or cryptogenic
top5.rationale: Hyperdense right M1 on unenhanced CT with corresponding CTA filling defect, plus lenticular/caudate hypodensity indicating infarct core, is the defining objective pattern; labs were unremarkable and no source was found.

top5.diagnosis: Paradoxical embolism via patent foramen ovale (PFO)
top5.rationale: A cryptogenic large-vessel embolic stroke in an elderly patient with no detected source should prompt evaluation for PFO/atrial septal defect; the negative hypercoagulable and cardiac workup supports this overlooked mechanism.

top5.diagnosis: Atrial fibrillation with cardioembolic stroke
top5.rationale: Cardioembolism is the most common mechanism for proximal MCA occlusion; however, the recorded ECG showed sinus rhythm, making this less likely but still possible if paroxysmal AF was not captured.

top5.diagnosis: Carotid or aortic arch atherosclerotic embolic stroke
top5.rationale: The CTA protocol screened great-vessel origins through the circle of Willis; absence of reported stenosis argues against, but large-artery atherosclerosis remains a plausible embolic source in a patient with hypercholesterolemia and prior smoking.

top5.diagnosis: Hypercoagulable state (e.g., antiphospholipid antibody syndrome) with large-vessel thrombosis
top5.rationale: Anticardiolipin IgG/IgM and lupus anticoagulant were negative, but activated protein C resistance screen was borderline/abnormal at 3.2, which could support a prothrombotic tendency if confirmed.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic melanoma (stage III/IV) with regional nodal and in-transit metastases
top5.rationale: Prior superficial spreading melanoma, biopsy-proven nodal metastasis, and hypermetabolic inguinal/iliac/thigh deposits form a single unifying explanation for all findings.

top5.diagnosis: Melanoma with incidental hypoglycemia (medication-related or fasting)
top5.rationale: Glucose 56 mg/dL is the only abnormal lab and is best explained by metoprolol/digoxin or fasting rather than a separate endocrine malignancy.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic melanoma with superimposed soft-tissue infection (cellulitis/lymphangitis)
top5.rationale: Initial erythema and swelling responded to cephalexin, suggesting a bacterial component accompanying the necrotic nodal mass.

top5.diagnosis: Second primary malignancy (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma or Merkel cell carcinoma) in an immunosuppressed/sun-damaged patient
top5.rationale: Extensive sun exposure and prior melanoma raise the possibility of a non-melanoma skin cancer mimicking nodal metastasis, though biopsy already confirmed melanoma.

top5.diagnosis: Paraneoplastic hypoglycemia (insulin-like growth factor-2 mediated) from bulky melanoma
top5.rationale: Non-islet cell tumor hypoglycemia is a rare but recognized complication of large metastatic melanoma burden and could explain the low glucose.

top5.diagnosis: Cardioembolic stroke due to occult paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
top5.rationale: The leading hypothesis (large-vessel atherosclerotic or cryptogenic stroke) leaves the embolic source unexplained; the negative workup and prior transient facial numbness suggest an intermittent embolic source that was never captured.

top5.diagnosis: Stroke due to paradoxical embolism via patent foramen ovale
top5.rationale: A young-at-heart 72-year-old with no vascular risk factors beyond hypercholesterolemia and no identified source could have a PFO with venous thrombus, which the workup did not exclude.

top5.diagnosis: Cervical artery dissection (traumatic or spontaneous)
top5.rationale: The fall the night before admission and the syncopal episode could have caused a dissection that embolized to the right MCA, and the CT angiography may not have fully evaluated the neck.

top5.diagnosis: Hypercoagulable state (e.g., antiphospholipid antibody syndrome or inherited thrombophilia)
top5.rationale: The thrombus in the MCA without a clear source, plus the family history of stroke, raises the possibility of a prothrombotic state that was not fully excluded by the limited coagulation workup.

top5.diagnosis: Incidental right MCA thrombus with an alternative explanation for the clinical syndrome (e.g., seizure with postictal Todd's paralysis)
top5.rationale: The syncopal episode and prior transient facial numbness could represent seizures, and the striking imaging finding may be an incidental companion finding rather than the sole cause of the presentation.

top5.diagnosis: Cardioembolic stroke due to occult atrial fibrillation
top5.rationale: 72-year-old with hypercholesterolemia, prior smoking, and family history of stroke; no source of embolism was found on routine workup, but paroxysmal AF is a common hidden cause of large-vessel MCA occlusion in this demographic.

top5.diagnosis: Large-artery atherosclerosis with in situ thrombosis of the right MCA
top5.rationale: Hypercholesterolemia and remote smoking are the only vascular risk factors; a ruptured plaque in the proximal right MCA could produce the hyperdense M1 clot without an embolic source.

top5.diagnosis: Transient ischemic attack preceding the stroke (left facial numbness 2 weeks and 2 days prior)
top5.rationale: The two episodes of 30-minute left lower facial numbness are classic heralding TIAs, indicating active unstable cerebrovascular disease and raising the pretest probability of a proximal embolic or thrombotic source.

top5.diagnosis: Hypercoagulable state (e.g., antiphospholipid antibody syndrome or inherited thrombophilia)
top5.rationale: The case explicitly sent protein C, protein S, anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant, and activated protein C resistance studies; a positive result would be an overlooked unifying explanation for arterial thrombosis in a patient with few conventional risk factors.

top5.diagnosis: Fall-related traumatic intracranial hemorrhage or cervical artery dissection
top5.rationale: Syncope with head strike the night before admission and a subsequent fall at symptom onset could have caused a traumatic dissection or hemorrhagic component; the cervical collar and trauma history are easy to dismiss once the hyperdense MCA sign is seen.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic melanoma (recurrent, regional nodal and in-transit)
top5.rationale: Prior superficial spreading melanoma with biopsy-proven nodal metastasis and hypermetabolic inguinal/iliac/thigh deposits fits direct lymphatic and in-transit spread; hallmark S100/SOX10/HMB-45 positivity and BRAF/NRAS mutations.

top5.diagnosis: Melanoma with hypoglycemia due to tumor burden (paraneoplastic/consumptive)
top5.rationale: Glucose 56 mg/dL without other cause suggests tumor-associated hypoglycemia (e.g., IGF-2 or consumptive), a mechanism easily overlooked when focused on staging.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic melanoma with incidental chronic lymphocytic leukemia/Small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL)
top5.rationale: Generalized lymphadenopathy in an older patient could reflect a second clonal B-cell process; flow cytometry showing CD5+/CD23+ monoclonal lymphocytes would be the clue.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic melanoma with immune-related adverse event or paraneoplastic neuropathy (hearing loss)
top5.rationale: Sensorineural hearing loss may be immune-mediated or paraneoplastic, supported by antineuronal antibodies or cochlear enhancement on MRI.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic melanoma with tumor lysis-like or infiltrative marrow involvement causing hypoglycemia
top5.rationale: Extensive nodal and possible marrow involvement could cause hypoglycemia via consumptive mechanisms; marrow biopsy and LDH/urate would support this.

top5.diagnosis: Metastatic melanoma (stage IV, regional nodal and likely distant)
top5.rationale: Biopsy-proven melanoma in right groin nodes with PET-CT hypermetabolism in external iliac, femoral, inguinal, and medial thigh nodes plus CT-enlarged retroperitoneal/pelvic nodes fits advanced metastatic disease.

top5.diagnosis: Hypoglycemia due to metastatic melanoma (non-islet cell tumor hypoglycemia)
